speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING OFF-SHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. In view of the lapse of time since the Supreme Court rendered its decision relating to mineral rights off the coast of British Columbia, is the Prime Minister able to inform us whether it is the intention of the government to proceed with any further references to the Supreme Court relating to mineral rights off the coast of other provinces or is the government now prepared to engage in negotiations with the provinces regarding offshore mineral rights.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING OFF-SHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
I believe there are two parts to the question. On the question of negotiation, Mr. Pearson had indicated that we did intend to reach equitable arrangements by negotiation with the provincial governments once the Supreme Court had established the law, as it has. These equitable arrangements will have to be found in negotiation with the provinces.
With regard to the position taken by other provinces in respect of Hudson Bay, our position is that the boundaries have been well defined by the 1912 act and that they follow the coast line of the provinces.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING OFF-SHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext: My question relating to other provinces does not necessarily relate to Hudson Bay but rather to possible differences with regard to the legal proposition. In view of the questions I put to his predecessor, the former prime minister, last winter requesting a declaration of intention on the part of the government concerning whether it intended to proceed with further references regarding rights in other provinces or whether it was prepared to engage in negotiations, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether in view of the lapse of time the government is now able to indicate to the house whether it intends to proceed by way of further legal proceedings or by negotiation.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING OFF-SHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext: I understand the question. We do not intend to proceed by further references. We intend to proceed by negotiation, and I will have a proposition for the provinces very soon.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING OFF-SHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question which relates to the underwater resources of Hudson Bay and the agreement reached by the governments of Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba to divide those resources among themselves.
In view of the statement by one of the provincial ministers to the effect that the provinces had been led to believe that "if we agree, the federal government would withdraw", will the Prime Minister now confide to the house and to the country the nature of any negotiations or undertakings given by the federal government to these three provinces in this regard?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS INQUIRY AS TO ACTION RESPECTING OFF-SHORE MINERAL RIGHTS
speechtext: No undertaking whatsoever has been given to these three provinces in this regard, but the offer to discuss the whole subject on an equitable basis is of course open to them. However, there has been no commitment by the federal government that it would do more than that.

What has happened since we last met in this house and discussed agriculture? The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Muir) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankow-ski) have put on the record evidence of the catastrophe that has befallen some segments of the industry. What do we find? Rather than farmers never having it so good, I point out that the sugar beet industry in Ontario has collapsed in 12 months. It no longer exists as an industry; it is finished. The fruit and vegetable industry is fighting for its very existence. In the great greenhouse industry of southwestern Ontario, which is concentrated mainly in Essex county, some of its most permanent establishments have gone into bankruptcy in the last few months. This event shook the whole economic climate of that area. The oilseed industry, faced with tremendous imports of edible oils, is trying desperately to find a solution to its problems in order that it may survive economically. Western grain growers have found grain piling up in the west and tremendous backlogs along the entire grain pipe line. The feed grain industry finds itself faced with overproduction and falling markets. The great corn industry in southwestern Ontario has found that the prices offered for this commodity are in many instances lower than the cost of production. These are the main segments of agriculture, the very backbone of the industry.
The federal government is supposed to encourage and develop the agricultural industry. What has happened? If you could have stood, as I did this summer, on one of the most progressive farms in southwestern Ontario, with an acreage of the finest head lettuce I have ever seen, and found that not one single head of that lettuce could be cut because there was absolutely no market for it at any price, if you could have stood on receiving platforms of farm co-operatives, as I did, and seen beautiful cabbage of top quality brought in, the very first offerings of the season, and found that the growers of this cabbage would receive for their produce as a starting price less than the price they received at the end of the last season, if you could have stood with me and seen a farmer leaning against a gate with tears in his eyes, watching the dispersal of a dairy herd which
The Address-Mr. Danjorth took three generations to establish; if you could have watched with me beside one of the largest and best buildings developed for the production of pork that I have ever seen, and have indicated to you by that farmer, a most progressive and businesslike man, that the entire operation had been shut down because the margin of profit would not even pay the interest on his investment; if you could have gone with me into a feed lot, which looked like blocks of pavement with its mangers, silos and automatic feeders, and found the feed lot empty because of lack of credit and lack of financial return, then you would realize, as I and my colleagues have done, that the agricultural industry of this great country is in dire straits.

It is no wonder that there is no levity any longer in the farming communities of this country. It is a sad thing indeed to go into a small farming community and find no gaiety or banter in the machine shops, no gathering of the ladies' groups at the local churches, no winter card parties, no dances, and no community life. Rather, there is an almost deathly silence, and the reason for this is that the farmer and his wife are out in the fields working from daylight to dark to try to increase their production in order to cope with falling prices. It is no fun to park your car in front of a bank and see farmers coming out one at a time, white-faced and shaken, knowing that they face bankruptcy or the curtailment of their business. It is no fun to read the daily newspapers and find column after column of advertised sales involving dispersal of herds, dispersal of farm lands and dispersal of farm machinery, and to know that these men will walk off their farms with their wives, their kiddies, their suitcases and nothing else after putting a whole lifetime of effort into the production on this land which they love so dearly. It is no answer to have the government say it will increase farm loans, give farmers a little more credit and set up a grains council and task forces. Something is wrong.
I wish to give the greatest of credit to the Economic Council of Canada and the men who form that great body for their insight into this problem. I want to pay tribute also to the men in the United States department of agriculture who are seized with this problem. These men have the facts. If the government cared to, it could read these facts. These men know how many men are moving off the farms. To speak of inefficiency on the farms

The time is past for us in this parliament to be content with using the old, hackneyed methods to solve the farm problems of today. Farmers today surely deserve a fair margin of profit for their labour and for their capital investment, equal to that of other segments of industry. If we could assure them that justice will be done there would be no farm problem and we would not be faced with these men leaving the farms. The tragedy is that the farm situation is so bad that farmers themselves are encouraging and almost insisting that their sons and daughters leave the farm and seek some other form of employment, no matter what it is. There is nothing that fills the heart with greater compassion than to see a man and a woman on a farm working from daylight to dark, barefooted in the mud, in a desperate attempt to get enough money to send their son or daughter to college in the hope they will not suffer the same fate as they have because they are farmers in Canada. We certainly cannot be proud of this situation.
The government of this country must take absolute responsibility for the plight of farmers today. I say this advisedly, not in a partisan manner but in the light of existing conditions today. We no longer speak of the law of supply and demand where farmers and their produce are concerned. We must speak of managed markets. It used to be possible for a provincial co-operative, in which farmers

united to act as a group, to exert some pressure, to have some control of sales and to demand a fair price in the marketplace. Today this is not possible because of the changing trade patterns.
What can a marketing group do when there are now cartels and international food chains capable of buying food at bargain prices anywhere in the world and through their own organizations distributing produce to any single locality in the world where there is a prime demand for it? All too often this is so in Canada. We are producing perhaps a 30 per cent surplus of which we must dispose in order for agriculture to survive as an industry, and at the same time the records show that each year we import over $800 million worth of food produce. My point is that not only do we have managed markets and cartels but we have government action which by a stroke of the pen can destroy a market in this country that farmers have tried for months to develop. This was one result of government action. Millions of bushels of commercial corn were imported into Canada just prior to our corn harvest last year. The market collapsed and our farmers had to take 30 or 40 cents a bushel less. It was found expedient to allow this corn to come into this country.

This does not put any money in the hands of the farmers. I say it is time the government began to show some backbone and started to think about Canada first. Within 24 hours other countries can impose a duty, in spite of the Kennedy accord, on our exports to them, so why can we not do the same? The government says we might offend the country in question. I do not believe that is so. I think we have to have a new

approach, the same approach as that used by labour, management and business. I say it is time the government of Canada talked to the governments of countries exporting to this country and discussed quotas or ways and means by which trade can be carried on that would be of benefit to both countries rather than a boon to one and a calamity to the other.

We expected to receive an indication in the throne speech that this would be done. We expected that the government would take an absolutely new approach to agriculture. They told us that is what they were going to do. We had no reason, other than their past performance, to doubt that they might. However, the speech from the throne and the Prime Minister's speech leave no doubt in the minds of the farmers of Canada that unless something drastic is done the great farming industry of this country will collapse. We are not going to solve the problem by moving farmers off the land.
If this government is under the mistaken belief that the consumers of this country are going to get any cheaper food if it is imported rather than produced here, may I say at once that will never come about. If anyone cares to follow the history of these matters he will find that once the local industry has been destroyed prices go up. I say, that we have had trading patterns. We have managed markets. We have restricted opportunities for sales in our own domestic market as a result of the amalgamation of companies. It is my opinion that in the case of some agricultural products offered on the Canadian market, the number of buyers has been reduced to about six or eight. There is no such thing as competition from supply and demand. We know that in many cases the price is an agreed price. The free enterprise idea in our agricultural economy is nothing but a myth.
I believe, therefore, that at this time this government should take a new look at agriculture. Here we are, a country that at one time was the envy of the world because we were constantly bringing out new varieties, new products, new methods of processing, shipping, storing and handling. Within a few years we find ourselves fighting for our very existence. We have the means and the research facilities. We have the Department of Agriculture. We have the facilities in this

Let us show some leadership. Let us show some activity. We have universities that can handle some of these problems. Mr. Speaker, it was a moving experience to take my place in this house amongst so many distinguished colleagues. It is with much diffidence that I rise for the first time. As did those who preceded me, Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate you and your deputies. May I also join with them in praising the mover (Mr. Corbin) and seconder (Mr. Marchand) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I wish to speak on the expropriation of land by the federal government.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
As a new member, may I refer briefly to the new riding of Peel South, whose constituents I have the honour to represent. We are faced with a problem which could arise in any riding, namely, the need to balance the
September 19, 19G8

The Address-Mr. Chappell rights of individuals against the requirements of government in expropriation cases.
The boundaries of Peel South roughly conform with those of Mississauga, one of the largest municipalities in Ontario. At the south we have Port Credit, a major terminal in the seaway system. At the north is Malton, dominated by the Toronto international airport. The area is now about 25 per cent developed, but it is well planned for future residential, commercial and industrial development. Its enormous potential, along with the regional importance of the ports, makes the municipality of Mississauga a major factor in our country's economic strength. The shortest look into the future affirms that these ports and other services will have to be enlarged, and this brings with it the inevitable expropriation of homes and other property. Expropriation does and will take place in every riding, but the imminence of substantial further taking of land to enlarge the airports at Malton and Montreal leads me to speak on this subject at the earliest possible moment.
As chairman of the comparative law section of the Canadian Bar Association I have been obliged to examine the laws of other jurisdictions, and while doing so I was struck by the fresh approaches being taken in other countries. Those countries which have not yet brought their expropriation laws up to date and in line with today's concepts of what is businesslike and just are rapidly doing so.
The Expropriation Act under which most federal expropriations take place was passed in 1889. Since then there has not been one amendment that affected the principle of expropriating property or the method of providing compensation.
The act was adequate for the social conditions and governmental requirements of 19th century Canada. Then expropriations were few, business was uncomplicated, land was plentiful and easily replaced with a minimum of disturbance to the owner.
Since the first world war social change has created the need for governments and their agencies to take more and more land. Concurrently other forces have striven to acquire and regulate land which is now relatively scarce in many areas. This tremendous increase in governmental expropriations has brought the subject into the spotlight of public attention. Today everyone could be affected, and everyone cringes at the thought. While not denying the need for governmental expropriation, owners rebel at the manner in which it is accomplished. To me, a member

representing one of the areas where new federal expropriation must take place, the shortcomings and antiquity of our act are most apparent.
What are these shortcomings?
No matter the complexity of the business being carried on or the extent of planning there may have been for expansion, there is no requirement that the owner be given notice of the intent to expropriate so that he may object and point out an error in choice or selection, or in the alternative adjust his plans.
Even when land is taken, which is done by the simple filing of a plan in the land registry office, the fundamental right of notice is not required; the owner is left to learn about it by chance. One wonders at this conflict with the bill of rights, which recognizes the right of an individual to enjoyment of property and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law.
There is no requirement for the government to pay or offer to pay all or any part of the compensation at the time of expropriation, or even when possession is demanded and taken. Unless some amount is offered voluntarily, the owner is left to try to reinstate himself without funds. Needless to say, he cannot borrow on the security of his property because he no longer owns it.
In the event that the owner is unable to settle with the authority, he does not have easy and speedy access to a tribunal to determine the compensation. He must proceed by a petition of right in the Exchequer Court, with which he is unfamiliar, with all of the delays, expenses and frustrations which arise when there are no safeguards against them.
There is no guide line for the method by which his loss shall be determined. This has been left to case law. The case law principles, which determine the amount of compensation, fluctuate. There are gaps and inconsistencies in the statutory provisions. For example, if an owner's property is damaged by reason of the construction of a public work on neighbouring land, he may recover compensation. But if his property is damaged by reason of the operation of that same public work, he may not recover his damages.
He is entitled to interest at 5 per cent after he has given up possession, but this is not payable until the amount of compensation is finally determined by the courts. The interest rate was reduced in 1900 from 6 per cent to 5 per cent, and after judgment the interest rate is reduced to 4 per cent. When an owner is
September 19, 1968	COMMONS
faced with paying 9 per cent mortgage interest on the land expropriated from him, and at the same time paying perhaps 10 to 12 per cent on money borrowed to try to relocate himself, such unfairness may force him to accept almost any offer.
Consider what can and does happen to an owner whose $18,000 home, which is subject to a mortgage for $12,000 at 7 per cent, is expropriated. If the authority should volunteer an advance of $9,000, say, all of this must be applied against the mortgage, leaving a balance of $3,000. Years later, when he receives the balance of his compensation, he must pay $23,000, say for his new home and be burdened with a mortgage of $17,000 at a higher interest rate. In the meantime he has had to continue to pay interest on the balance of the existing mortgage on the land taken, but he receives only 5 per cent from the authority. For all practical purposes he is deprived of a home, or at least one which he can afford.
Or if an owner who has a small home worth, say, $10,000, with a mortgage on it for $8,000, accepts an offer of $10,000, he usudlly cannot replace his home for less than $12,000 to $15,000 simply because of the inadequate supply of homes in this price range. Thus he suffers a loss for which he was not responsible. Just last week an owner who lost such a home in Halifax paraded on our lawn protesting such treatment. He and others in his position expect expropriated homes to be replaced with similar ones.
Although an owner's land is invaded and diminished in value by an expropriation of part of it, or an easement over it or through it, such as landing equipment around an airport, he cannot call on the authority to take it all, as is the practice in England.
Although an owner's land may be depreciated in value because of general knowledge of pending expropriation-generally referred to by text writers as pre-expropriation blight-his compensation is set as of the date of expropriation without any allowance for reduction, which may be very substantial and was caused by the authority. In England such an allowance is made.
Hon. J. C. McRuer, retired chief justice of the high court in Ontario, in his royal commission report to the government of Ontario quoted Hon. J. Thorson, then President of the Exchequer Court who, in dealing with a federal expropriation, said in a judgment in 1956:
I am not aware of any other country in the civilized world that exercises its right of eminent

I hope I have sufficiently directed the attention of hon. members to this problem,

The Address-Mr. O'Connell that we may immediately bring our expropriation laws more in line with ordinary concepts of reason and justice and thus lead the way for the provinces and perhaps ultimately lead to uniform expropriation codes for all parts of Canada.
I have full confidence in this government and believe that if defects in our laws are pointed out they will be corrected. In this case there is an urgency. In British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Ontario expropriation laws have been under review and are being changed. This is our opportunity to do more than patch up existing legislation. We must develop a new concept of compensation which will speedily put a man in the same relative position that he was in before government required his property or government activity affected it. If we act promptly our legislation may have the additional advantage of influencing the provincial legislatures before their new acts are passed.
The task is not as great as it may appear. England has kept her expropriation laws up to date for the last 120 years. New Zealand and Pennsylvania recently brought theirs up to date. In British Columbia and Ontario Hon. J. V. Clyne and Hon. J. C. McRuer have studied the whole subject and made detailed recommendations.
I understand from the Minister of Justice that a new act will be brought forward, but in the meantime, I am sure that the people of Peel South and all Canadians who are affected by expropriation may have the assurance of this government that everything possible will be done that may be done within the framework of existing legislation to relieve against the present deficiencies in our legislation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
May I begin, Mr. Speaker, by congratulating you on your re-election and by congratulating Mr. Deputy Speaker and the Deputy Chairman of Committees for being elected to the important offices they hold. I also wish to congratulate the hon. members for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin) and Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) for their excellent statements in moving and seconding the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I have the honour to represent the newly created riding of Scarborough East, situated on the eastern boundary of metropolitan Toronto. The residents of my riding were formerly in the riding of York-Scarborough and
[Mr. Chappell.}
were so ably represented in the previous parliament by the hon. member who now represents York-Scarborough. On behalf of my constituents and on my own behalf may I congratulate the hon. member on his appointment as parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State. In a previous parliament my constituents-and they well remember this -enjoyed the energetic and distinguished representation of Mr. M. J. Moreau.
As hon. members know, the borough of Scarborough for the past decade has undergone exceptional growth. It may well double in population in the next 15 years. The eastern portion of the borough, that part covered by the constituency of Scarborough East, is growing even more rapidly and promises to double in population in the next five years. Much of the undeveloped land remaining in Metro Toronto lies in the constituency of Scarborough East and the pressures for residential and industrial development are extremely high. Indeed, five areas within the new constituency, each of which will result in communities of between 20,000 and 30,000 persons, are in various stages of development.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
One such area is the federal-provincial land assembly scheme at Malvern, involving some 1,800 acres acquired 15 years ago in 1953 but on which the first housing is expected to appear only in 1970. Hon. members will appreciate the severe strains caused by such growth, not only in blending new areas with established communities but also the strains on municipal finances in providing water and sewer services, schools, recreation facilities, public transportation and other services. In a constituency such as mine, residents come to realize the limitations of many urban municipalities as presently organized, administered and financed to meet growth problems, and accordingly they expect greater initiatives from the provincial government, particularly in lifting a more substantial part of educational costs from local property taxation. They expect also a better co-ordination of federal, provincial and municipal functions than, for example, has been evident in the tragically slow development at Malvern even in the face of a mounting housing crisis.
They expect new policies and programs from the federal government to cope with growth problems in such fields as inter-city transportation, rapid transit, pollution control, housing, basic utilities, and the creation of new towns within regional development
September 19, 1968	COMMONS
plans to relieve pressures on existing metropolitan areas. I will not expand on urban problems, Mr. Speaker, but I do hope to have an opportunity, together with provincial and municipal elected representatives in my constituency, to place a brief before the task force on housing and urban affairs when it visits metro Toronto at the end of this month.
I would like today to offer some thoughts and proposals for the development of policy in Indian affairs. I appreciate this is an extremely complex field, and though I have some small background in it I know there are many hon. members here more qualified by experience than I to speak on it because of the presence in their ridings of Indian communities. But I believe we were all encouraged to enter upon these problems by the references in the throne speech to Indians, to the righting of wrongs and the opening of new opportunities, and by the high priority placed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), shared by all hon. members, on the eradication of poverty and the attainment among us of a higher order of justice.
There is in Indian affairs in Canada a new citizen frontier. It is there because Indian citizens are now making a collective decision to integrate with general society. We cannot view this as anything less than a major turning point in the history of the new world. In our generation we are seeing a transformation of the life of native citizens, the giving up of historic communal isolation, as Indians come to see that taking possession of this land again really means sharing in the making of its future, and come to see that only by sharing in making a common future can they repossess themselves as full men and women and, as contemporary Canadians, be assured of retaining an Indian identity. That collective decision and turning point and our response to them are the new frontiers of opportunity and obligation opening before us in this parliament.
How are we to play our part? Let me begin by stating two basic assumptions that underlie what I propose to say. The first is that Indians in the main do wish to integrate with the general stream of Canadian life, to share fully in it as equal citizens but not to assimilate in the sense of disappearing as Indians. They seek to integrate as individuals and as entire communities while retaining a sense of communal or ethnic identity.
The second assumption is that the reservation community will remain the permanent
DEBATES	215
The Address

Mr. O'Connell base of Indian community life for the foreseeable future, hopefully in a modified and more developed form. I will not stop here to defend these positions but I do wish to make them explicit because unless each of us defines his attitude on these two basic questions he will, with respect, Mr. Speaker, be unable to help shape successful public policy, and will be unable to assist Indians to build those internal strengths and programs of self-help vital to progress.
Before suggesting some specific proposals in such areas as economic development I would like to recall very briefly to hon. members some facts concerning the situation of Indians in Canada today.
The more than 225,000 registered Indians of Canada belong to some 556 bands living in over 2,000 reserve communities set aside by treaty over the past 100 years for their exclusive use and designed to support a traditional way of life. Many reservations have populations under 100 persons. However, 60 per cent of Canada's Indians, and over 70 per cent of Ontario's 55,000 Indians, live in communities with populations ranging between 500 and 2,000, with the exception of the Six Nations reserve near Brantford of approximately 8,000 persons.
These larger communities, as well as certain smaller ones, offer opportunities for economic and social development. However, not only have they been isolated from the mainstream of social and economic life, they have also been insulated from each other by language differences, inertia, poverty and physical distance. A wide range in the level of cultural development separates Indians from each other.
Internal divisions arise within communities as to the best course to follow, and the lack of effective local government machinery capable of developing a working consensus further impedes action. To meet the wide variety of needs under these circumstances there are required special and flexible approaches not yet available under the existing Indian Act nor, I would add, under the present structure of the Indian affairs branch.
The outstanding fact of Indian life is poverty. Indian poverty is self-perpetuating. It goes around in a circle that has not been broken in a century. No matter where one enters the circle, at the point of education, or at the points of health, housing, employment, community development, pride in self, or motivation, one is led from one point to the other
216	COMMONS DEBATES	September 19/ 1968
The Address-Mr. O'Connell
around the full circle. The circularity of Indian poverty and the inter-penetration of one condition with another surely means that only a broad, comprehensive approach can succeed in raising standards of life and personal development in keeping with current Indian expectations. The new Indian initiatives and the historical decision to integrate, to which I referred earlier, hold out the brightest promise in centuries that the cycle of poverty, with our help, can be broken in our generation.
You are already familiar with the main measures of the gulf of poverty across which Indian citizens live, and I will not review them here. Another fact of Indian life as important to us as poverty, and perhaps more important in its implications for a future of justice and development, is the sense of grievance and injustice harboured in many Indian communities. Again I do not intend to dwell upon this subject this afternoon apart from expressing the hope that the Indian lands claims commission bill will be introduced early in this parliament and, further, that we will deem it urgent and proper to amend the Migratory Birds Convention Act, passed by parliament 50 years ago and which, however unwittingly, did abridge and violate the hunting rights of Indians agreed to in solemn treaties.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
I wish to turn now to some specific proposals which may contribute to progress. The first may be summed up as a plan for the economic development of Indian communities through industry and employment. Surely opportunities for gainful employment must rank in the forefront of all plans. One need not deny the central importance of education, but we tend to believe that education will solve all problems. Education is only one point on the circle. The essential point, I believe, is that success in other programs, like housing, welfare, health and general community development, depends to a major degree on building economies capable of supporting such programs and services. If we are to be serious about Indian communities and their self-reliance and not expect them simply to wither away, then we must integrate them as viable communities more closely with the mainstream, with standards of life approximating the general standard. This means attempting to create economic activity on or near reserves, wherever feasible, capable of providing employment and developing the community. In fact, as I see it a systematic program of economic development, such as I

propose to describe, provides the essential incentives as well as the means for other developments. Let me suggest the outlines of such a plan to replace the present weak, scattered and unco-ordinated programs of low capability.
To achieve economic development in difficult circumstances, there should be established an economic development agency closely related to, though not necessarily located within, the Indian affairs branch and staffed with professional, technical and development personnel, including Indians. Such an agency should administer an economic development fund of perhaps $25 million but be charged with more than mere lending functions. It would, for example, with the collaboration of the band councils, undertake feasibility studies for industrial enterprises of various kinds on or near reserve communities. It would undertake an evaluation of natural and human resources of Indian communities; it would make repayable loans and certain nonrepayable grants to assist in the promotion of industrial projects of Indian bands, co-operatives, individual Indians and approved nonIndian persons. The development agency, with the approval of band councils, would be prepared to supply technical and management personnel at certain stages of project development. With the approval of band councils, the development agency should encourage companies to locate certain operations on or near reserves to expand employment opportunities.
The agency should also seek to arrange with major Canadian industries to provide on-job training programs for selected Indian workers and be prepared to share in the wage and other costs of such programs. The agency should assume job placement functions and work in close co-operation with the manpower centres and existing vocational and technical training programs. It should co-ordinate and ensure the extension to reserve communities of existing development programs such as ARDA and FRED, the area development programs, and of provincial programs. An important function would be to conduct a study of credit available to Indians and to encourage savings and credit institutions in reserve communities.
Such is a brief outline of a development agency supported by substantial development funds and specialist personnel. It is designed to do a comprehensive job, recognizing that existing programs and facilities fail to meet
September 19, 1968	COMMONS
the special needs of Indian citizens, and recognizing also that industry and employment are basic foundations for success in most other fields. An essential requirement in complex development fields is for an agency more flexible than a government department and more capable of tapping provincial and other resources.
I should also like to draw the attention of the house to another salient in the new frontier-the need to encourage mutual aid associations, self-help and other organizations among Indians and Eskimos. Such voluntary agencies and groups proliferate in general society but only now begin to emerge among Canada's native people. Not only do we too often fail to encourage Indians to establish such groups, we fail to support those that do emerge. Consider for a moment the importance to individual pride and group solidarity of the aid organizations developed by immigrants. The civil rights movement, for example, has been a powerful force creating group pride and self-improvement. Indians need such mutual help organizations. The evidence,
I believe, is that group and individual pride and dignity are directly relevant to integration.
I would like to advance a proposal designed to bring assistance to Indian organizations and to serve an essential purpose in the cultural field which is so directly related to the question of Indian identity. This proposal, which is for the creation of a Canada Indian institute, is made as a response to Indian appeals and initiatives particularly on the part of Indian youth. Among the characteristics of a Canada Indian institute, as I see them, are the following.
It should be an autonomous national body established by the federal government upon the request, preferably, of a national conference of Indian people. Its relations with the federal government should be similar to those of independent councils and crown corporations, for example, the Canada Council. Its board of governors should be composed of Indians, Metis and other citizens. Its financing should be based largely on government funds but it should also actively solicit private funds from foundations, corporations and individuals.
Among the interlocking functions and activities of the proposed Canada Indian institute should be these: first, to affiliate with the Inter-American Indian Institute. This is an international body formed in 1940 and supported by some 18 member countries but
DEBATES	217
The Address-Mr. O'Connell not by Canada, I may say. It serves as a clearing house for information on Indian developments and on the methods of improving their social and economic conditions. There is no doubt in my mind that Canadian affiliation with the Inter-American Indian Institute would be of significant advantage to Indians of Canada. It seems to me there is every reason to expect that Canada's external aid program should include aid to other countries to assist in the development of Indian communities throughout this hemisphere and for cultural exchanges between Canadian and other Indian groups. Canada might indeed, a few years hence, become the host country to an international congress of Indian and other native people of this hemisphere to the great advantage of Canadian citizens, not only those of Indian and Eskimo ancestry. On the cultural plane alone, though I would add the political and social planes also, the native people of Canada have much to contribute to such a gathering. We know, for example, that some of the high art of the hemisphere has been produced by Indians of the northwest coast of Canada.
Another function of the Canada Indian institute would be to assist Indian, Metis and Eskimo organizations to develop, operate, assist, for example, and finance up to some reasonable point such organizations as the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians, the B. C. Native Brotherhood, the Union of Ontario Indians, the Alberta Metis Federation, the Manitoba Metis Association, the Quebec Indian Association, the Canadian Indian Youth Council, and the Canadian Indian Brotherhood. I mention only a few among many examples of regional, provincial and national native organizations. These organizations need financial aid to provide themselves with a small secretariat, to engage expert legal and other consultants, and to meet as organizations, and with other associations, in order to overcome decades of isolation as well as to examine problems and goals sufficiently to make solid contributions to development and to share in the decisions affecting their lives. It should be possible for government to contract certain community development functions to such Indian organizations since many of them can do the job better than government agencies.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
Another function should be to establish a technical and a consulting group within the institute to provide educational services, research, much needed legal, financial and
September 19, 1968

The Address-Mr. O'Connell other advisory services to Indian and Eskimo communities and organizations.
The institute should sponsor an extensive travel program for Indian youth and adults on visits to other Indian communities and to other parts of Canada to familiarize them with their opportunities. It could and should assist in holding in Canada an annual Canadian Indian conference lasting perhaps one week and attended by representatives of all native communities and organizations, assisted by expert personnel. The holding of such annual conferences managed by native people and free from direct sponsorship by government would undoubtedly result in a growing self-confidence and consensus among native people as to their own goals in the days to come. It should result in an authoritative body of Indian people capable of enlightening the people of Canada and in influencing the course of future public policy.
The institute should undertake special programs to foster cultural development of Indian communities and cultural activity in the performing and expressive arts. This is a neglected area in Canada. Programs lack cultural focus and they falter. The new and promising cultural affairs section of the Indian affairs branch has subsided. The cultural field is one in which North American governments appear confused and unfamiliar, hence the need of a definite action capability on the part of the proposed Canadian Indian institute.
The objective must be to encourage native people to keep vital and to keep reworking those universal and particular elements in their cultural patterns that will assist them to participate fully in contemporary life while retaining their basic Indian or Eskimo identities.
Cultural development turns the key to community and general social development. We tend to forget this. It is here that internal strengths are generated, that a sense of communal identity and individual pride are rooted, and it is here also that native citizens make valued and unique contributions to the many cultural streams in the Canadian pattern. We can no longer conceal from ourselves, if we know what Canada means, that through indifference on the one hand or repression on the other, a people was deeply wounded through undermining the cultural source of their lives. If we are not blind, therefore, we will put in the highest category,


above education, above economic development and above housing, freedom and support for those cultural rights and needs, whether in the performing or expressive arts, in language or other cultural modes which Indian and Eskimo people themselves determine to be the basic nourishment of their being.
The institute should assist in establishing a Canadian Indian college, an institution largely unhampered with regulations as to previous academic requirements but geared rather to a flexible learning process and devoted to studies in Indian history, social and moral values, cultural patterns and attainments, and to their application to the needs of native people in the contemporary world.
I have been suggesting some rather specific new approaches and institutional arrangements in the development of policies in Indian affairs. I should like to conclude by telling hon. members that some months ago I had the duty, when president of the Indian-Eskimo Association of Canada, of writing to the then Prime Minister expressing concern at the underachievement and the apparent subsidizing of the community development program. I have to reiterate here that same concern regarding the non-realization of the great potential of that program.
At that time the association recommended the appointment of a task force-they have since proliferated-to examine the status of the community development program and to consider the feasibility of establishing an Indian development corporation capable of fulfilling complex social and economic roles not readily open to government departments.
The association recommended also high level discussions between the Prime Minister and the premiers of the provinces, believing that only when the provinces faced up to. their constitutional and moral responsibilities to extend their services and development programs to reserve communities would reai progress be attainable.
I would like here to renew this request for a ministerial task force and state that in my opinion the most important step that could be taken at this time is to engage Indian communities, Indian organizations and individuals as well as provincial authorities an other agencies in a sustained consultation to study the whole question in all its aspects so that new directions may emerge.
There is a tangled web of conflicting jurisdictions; there is an uncertain approach to responsibilities to Indians, Metis and
September 19, 19G8	COMMONS
Eskimos, and there is also a failure to consider the problems of urban and urban bound native peoples. There is a pressing question of restoring and upholding treaty provisions, the proper roles of such public service organizations as the C.B.C. and the National Film Board. There is also the question of the relevance of the present structure and functions of the Indian affairs branch to the changing needs of today and other matters on which a working body of information and knowledge independent of that now possessed almost as a monopoly in the Indian affairs branch would prove valuable to hon. members as they consider the role of this parliament in Indian affairs.
What I am suggesting is that the commendable start being made in the present consultations regarding changes in the Indian Act be followed by broadened consultations with Indians on matters they wish to have discussed so that they will in fact experience a direct participation and involvement in decisions affecting their lives and ours, as well as discussions with other relevant and responding resources, principally the provinces. This should not be another lengthy study by academics, valuable as that may be, but a study by a small task force touring the country and developing recommendations on policy and programs to guide this house in the steps I feel sure it will want to take at the earliest opportunity.
By suggesting a few initiatives I hope I have indicated a few of the considerations which such a task force might investigate.
It is my conviction that no group of citizens can in fact take greater strides to help us all create a just society than can the Indian peoples of Canada. We have not been listening to Indian citizens or responding to their needs. We can unite our futures in equality. An unrivalled opportunity to do so lies now before this parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to congratulate you on your election to the position of Speaker of the house. I have heard others describe your ability in superlative terms and I am sure that these descriptions are accurate. However, since I have had the pleasure of meeting Your Honour only recently and observing your direction of the house for a short period of time, I would simply like to say that I am impressed with your pleasantness, fairness and stability.
DEBATES	219
The Address-Mr. Yewchuk [DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I am told that it is customary to confine the remarks contained within one's first speech to matters pertaining to one's constituency and therefore I intend to speak in that light. The constituency of Athabasca is the largest in the province of Alberta and is situated in the northeastern section of that province. It contains approximately 55,000 people and a variety of natural and human resources. At present probably the largest functioning industry of the constituency is agriculture. However, since the Athabasca tar sands are located in the riding and the oil refining facilities which are being developed at Fort McMurray are progressing, the possibility of oil refining becoming the largest industry in the near future is quite great.
There are also vast forest reserves in the riding. Wood Buffalo park is contained within the riding, and in Wood Buffalo park there are approximately 17,000 buffalo, together with minerals and other natural resources. The population of Athabasca, as I have mentioned, is quite varied. There are approximately 25 Indian reservations and several Metis colonies. Therefore problems pertaining to Metis and Indians are of great importance to me.
There are no cities contained in the riding. The major population centres, starting from west to east, are the towns of Peace River, High Prairie, High Level, Fort Vermilion, Slave Lake, Lac La Biche, Fort McMurray, Bonnyville, Elk Point, Cold Lake and Grand Centre containing the Canadian forces base. The largest towns are Peace River and Fort McMurray. Because the riding is so vast, with widespread population centres, there are many problems. Isolation is a great factor contributing to problems in the more northerly sections, since road construction in the north has been rather slow and many areas are accessible only by air with any ease.
The major problems in the riding as I see them, and about which I wish to speak, fall into three categories. The first, of course, is agriculture; the second, poverty and unemployment, with particular reference to Indians, Metis and small farmers. In this category I would like to include housing, unemployment and health and welfare. The third major problem is that of isolation, with subheadings of communications, particularly in reference to the construction of roads, and radio and television services.
I would like, therefore, to begin with the problems of agriculture. Most of the farms in
September 19, 1968

The Address-Mr. Yewchuk the Athabasca riding are of the mixed variety. The average farm consists of about 200 to 300 acres under cultivation. Because of soil conditions in that part of the country, and because of the economic state in which agriculture is today, this acreage is not sufficient to constitute an economic farming emit. According to the Alberta department of agriculture, somewhere in the vicinity of 600 acres of cultivated land is required to make a functioning, economic farm unit.
The greatest single factor which has contributed to making these small farms uneconomical is the fact that the price of farm products has not risen in the past 15 to 20 years. I am referring in particular to the price of wheat, hogs and beef. On the other hand, the price of farm machinery has more than doubled during this period. We might use as an example a tractor which pulls a three-bottom plow. In 1950 this machine could be purchased for about $2,500. Today the same tractor sells for somewhere between $5,000 and $6,000. Because of this unhealthy economic situation, many small farms are being abandoned.
In general it appears that the small family farm is becoming obsolete and is on the way out. But I question whether this is the best solution to the farm problem. Not every farmer wishes to give up his small farm. Many people who live on farms enjoy rural living and do not want to move to cities; yet because of unhealthy economic circumstances they are forced to do so.
Shortly after the election, when it became apparent that a party other than mine would form the government, I was asked by many whether there would be anything I, as an opposition member, could do in order to reach a solution to the problems which exist in the constituency. My reply was that I would try to promote what I thought were good ideas and that I would support anything the government did which I believed would be good for the area. I said I would oppose only those things which I thought would not be good for the area or the country.
With this in mind, I wish to say that I do support one of the things which is being done to aid the plight of the farmer. I am referring in particular to the functions of the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act or ARDA, which is already in operation. I am bringing ARDA into the picture at this point because the act is set up to assist rural communities to improve their economic status.

Naturally, the farmer who is running a small, uneconomic farming unit should qualify for some sort of assistance through the ARDA program.
As I have mentioned, many people are giving up their small farms and some are enlarging their operations. The principles of ARDA are to help those who wish to enlarge their farms to purchase other, developed land or to clear and open new land. The ARDA program is also aimed at helping those who wish to give up their farms in order to be retrained and relocated in other jobs. This, in theory, sounds beautiful, but in actual fact the program is not working that way. The machinery of the ARDA program seems to be in great need of lubrication. It is ponderous and does not function effectively.
Only about two weeks ago I met with farm leaders in one of the areas of the constituency. They had attempted to deal with ARDA for the past couple of years. One of the projects, which was applied for more than a year ago, pertained to increasing the cultivated acreage. This was to be done through clearing and opening new land which existed on their farms. More than a year had gone by and nothing had been done to consider this project up to the time of our meeting. About three months ago some farmers applied to have their land assessed and sold through the ARDA program, and again nothing has been done to date.
The machinery of ARDA is set up in such a way that any given project proposed by a local community must go through five committees before it obtains final approval. The first of these committees is composed of ordinary provincial civil servants. If they approve the application it goes to a provincial deputy ministers' committee, then to a provincial cabinet committee and then to a committee in Winnipeg. Finally it gets to a committee here in Ottawa, which gives it final approval. If it takes more than one year to get by the first committee, how long will it take for a project to receive final approval? I am raising this matter because it is of some urgency. When ARDA was first described in my constituency farmers saw it as a ray of hope, but they are becoming disillusioned because of the slowness of the machinery.
Within the past six months, in one poll alone in the constituency it was found that 12 farmers had given up their small farms, but there was no ARDA assistance available to them for relocation, retraining or anything
September 19, 1968

else. The program I have just discussed pertains mainly to farmers who are in great distress, but those who are not in as great distress also have many problems. I have already mentioned one of these problems, namely, the high price of farm machinery. I am therefore anxiously awaiting the report of the Barber commission and hope it will contain recommendations which will provide some element of stability with regard to the price of farm machinery in relation to the price of farm products.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The most glaring problem that farmers face today is that of the disposal of their products, particularly wheat. I am sure everyone is aware of the importance of wheat sales, and I am sure that any hon. member who has wheat farmers in his constituency will probably speak on this subject and will agree that action toward an aggressive world wide wheat policy as a long term solution to the farm problem is necessary, while a short term solution would be to make larger advance payments to the farmers for farm stored wheat. For example, I should like to see more of Canada's foreign aid be in the form of provision of food, particularly wheat, to other countries to a greater extent than has been done in the past. For instance, India alone has an annual birth rate of 21 million and is acutely short of food. Other far eastern countries are also short of food while we in our country have a vast surplus of food supply. It should be possible to neutralize these two great disparities in some way and at the same time to relieve problems of food shortage and lack of markets for our products.
The next major problem in the constituency which I wish to discuss is that of poverty and unemployment. As I mentioned before, it applies mainly to Indians, Metis and small farmers, but also to others. Along with this topic I might refer to the question of housing as it applies to my constituency. Reservations located in my constituency, as well as the Metis colonies which exist there, do not appear to be self-supporting at the present time. There appears to be insufficient capital on these lands to develop the land for agricultural use, and at the same time there are not sufficient numbers of other jobs on these lands to employ the people who live on them. This unhealthy situation contributes to a chronic condition of poverty, unemployment and underemployment with all its associated side effects.
The Address-Mr. Yewchuk
It soon became apparent to me in my travels during the campaign through most of the reservations and Metis colonies that the majority of Metis and Indians live in houses that are not fit for human habitation. I hasten to add, however, that there are occasional houses which are reasonably satisfactory. Because of poor housing conditions, overcrowding is very common. Poor water supply or no water supply is common. Many people living on reserves and colonies drink water from sloughs, lakes and streams. This type of drinking water is a definite health hazard and therefore dysentery is quite common among the children. Because of poor housing, overcrowding and undernourishment, the rate of tuberculosis in these areas is higher than nearly anywhere else in the country.
Many factors must be considered in order to try to improve the status of the poor in our area. When one considers that the Athabasca riding is probably the richest in Canada in natural resources-and again I am referring to the Athabasca tar sands-it is difficult to accept the fact that it probably also contains the largest number of poverty-stricken people of any constituency in the country. Many of our people who are in the poverty-stricken state are, of course, receiving provincial welfare, while some of the Indian people receive welfare from the federal Indian department. However, this is no way of solving the problem of poverty. The method of doling out welfare adopted today probably originated with Robin Hood. The idea is to solve poverty by taking from the rich and giving to the poor. Here it is taken from those who have by the government and given to the poor by the government. But this does not solve the problem of poverty; it simply prolongs it. A poor person cannot be made not poor by a gift of money because once he spends the money he is poor again. Therefore I feel that giving people outright welfare is only a good temporary solution but is not a satisfactory long term solution to the poverty problem.
It seems to me that in order to eliminate poverty on a long term basis, resource development is required, and I am referring to development of human resources as well as natural resources. Human resources must be developed in such a way that a person can then look after his own needs on a permanent basis, and natural resource development must be carried out simultaneously in order to give him opportunity for employment in his home area.
222	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Yewchuk
The greatest factors contributing to poverty and unemployment in my constituency are lack of education, lack of trade skills and lack of jobs. These, of course, result in part from isolation, as mentioned before. So in order for a long term solution to be found, the poverty-stricken population must be assisted to develop to the point where they can eventually look after themselves. Therefore isolation must be removed, either by bringing training facilities to isolated posts or by moving isolated populations en masse to areas where they could develop their own potential, or else a combination of these two suggestions could be used.
However, education is only one factor in solving the problem of poverty. There are many others to be considered, such as community development programs, preventive social service programs, and the reassessment of the welfare program as it exists today. The reassessment of the welfare program is necessary because the present set-up discourages people from trying to look after themselves. A certain earning level is considered necessary to feed, clothe and shelter a family of a given size, and if a man earns a given number of dollars, then the difference between his earnings and his need is made up by the welfare department. However, if he earns less, then he simply gets more from the welfare department, and if he earns nothing he gets all from the welfare department. Sooner or later this encourages such people to earn nothing because they see no point in working when, if they do not, all of the money will come from welfare anyway.
I am not saying that this happens in the case of all welfare recipients, but am merely trying to point out the fact that the program as it exists takes away the motivation and the ambition of poor people to look after themselves. Therefore I suggest that the program be altered and that welfare assistance be given as a percentage of what a person earns or can earn after his earning potential and his needs have been considered so that to a certain extent, if he earns more he would get more from the welfare department. This would at least make him more motivated to continue seeking employment, however temporary it may be.
It has also been observed in my constituency where new industrial development is taking place at Fort McMurray that this does not necessarily solve the problems of unemployment in the area because many of the unemployed or underemployed are not trained for

DEBATES	September 19, 1968
the jobs which are available, and also because many of them have poor working habits and cannot hold jobs for long. As a result, people from other parts of the country are brought in to fill the jobs and the local unemployment problem remains the same. Therefore, in order that industrial development in that area can succeed in removing the unemployment problem, a co-operative effort must be made involving both the needs of the industry and the development of educational facilities. I wish to point out that there is a program of this nature in Lac-la-Biche. It is called Alberta Newstart Incorporated, and is designed to upgrade the way of living of the inhabitants in the area and to increase the earning potential of the unemployed and the underemployed. I feel this is a good scheme and I give it my wholehearted support. I wish to assure the minister responsible that I will do everything I can to ensure the success of this program.
I know that at the present time the Indian Act is under review and hearings are being held across the country with representatives of various Indian bands. I do not claim to be a good spokesman for Indians. I was told by an Indian once that it takes an Indian to really understand another Indian and his needs. However, from my conversations with many Indians it is my conclusion that Indians should be given as much autonomy as possible in the management of their own affairs. I feel that for too long the Indian has not been given enough credit for his ability to manage his affairs. May I remind the house that he managed quite well before the white man ever got here. In many areas there exist distorted views of what the Indian really is. Some people consider him to be subhuman and treat him accordingly. Some people do not know that he has the same needs, feelings, emotions and potentials as any other human being. I feel that if an Indian is given a chance to manage his own affairs, he will do more to solve his own problems than can anyone else.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The final major point for discussion is the problem of isolation and lack of communication plaguing large sections of the constituency. It is urgently necessary that the roads to resources program in the north of a previous government be resumed in its original or in a modified form. Road construction through these northern areas, starting from Fort McKay, which is north of Fort McMurray, to
September 19, 1968

Wood Buffalo park, with a branch to Chipew-yan and then continued to join the highway to Fort Smith on the Northwest Territories border should be continued without delay. There has been delay in construction because of negotiations taking place between the federal and Alberta governments with regard to the boundaries of Wood Buffalo park. If the boundaries remain the same, and if the road must go through Wood Buffalo park, then the federal government is responsible for construction of the road within the park. The provincial government, of course, would be responsible for those roads outside the park's boundaries. I suggest that since negotiations concerning the boundaries have been going on for so long without reaching a definite conclusion, the federal government should go ahead with the construction of that part of the road which falls within Wood Buffalo park. This should be done in conjunction with the feasibility studies the provincial government is now undertaking concerning the best location for the road.
Once the road to Fort Chipewyan is built, then it could be extended to Uranium City in co-operation with the Saskatchewan government. Some communications on this subject between the two governments have already taken place. In any event, construction of this type of road would certainly be a great boom to further industrial development in that area, as well as in relieving the acute isolation of many settlements at the present time. While we are on the topic of Wood Buffalo park and the road, this may be the appropriate time to suggest that industrial development of mineral resources in Wood Buffalo park would then proceed. This development would provide employment for many of the residents in that region, particularly around Fort Chipewyan.
I wish to mention another type of communication at this time, and that is television and radio service to northern areas. The town of Fort McMurray has no television. The towns of High Level and Fort Vermillion do not have television service or satisfactory radio reception. Fort McMurray contains about 6,000 people, while High Level and Fort Vermillion combined contain approximately 4,000. The growth potential for these towns is good, and I would urge the development of facilities for these towns immediately.
C.B.C. television could be brought to Fort McMurray through Lac La Biche, and to Fort Vermillion and High Level through the towns of Peace River and Manning, thus servicing
29180-15a
The Address-Mr. Yewchuk large population centres. The lack of television facilities in these northern towns contributes a great deal to the feeling of isolation. I know consideration is being given to satellite transmission of television in the north. I certainly hope this materializes. One way or another, I feel it is urgent that television service be provided within the next year. Television facilities in these areas would create better recreational opportunities and would be informative as well as educational.
I should like to give an example of what I mean. During the campaign, about two or three weeks before election day, I went to meet people in some isolated areas and introduced myself as a candidate in the coming election. Not uncommonly, the reply was "what election?" This certainly brought out what lack of communication means in a given area.
In recent months we have heard numerous eructations of the phrase "just society". I wish to make some comments on this. This term has been heard often, yet the originator of the term has never really defined this so-called just society. Does it mean socialism or does it mean greater emphasis on free enterprise? Does it mean social measures aimed only in the direction of the greatest need? I hope it does not mean the creation of general, socialistic measures. I hope it does not mean socialism because I feel that if any justice in our society is to exist it has to be based on a foundation of maximum freedom for the individual. Individual freedom was mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. Justice or a just society cannot exist without a foundation of individual freedom because if across the board social welfare measures are introduced on a compulsory basis this takes away one's freedom of choice in two ways, freedom of choice whether or not one wants' the measure and freedom of choice whether or not one wants to pay for it. I hope, therefore, that in a just society humanitarian programs will be designed only for those who are in need and that freedom of choice will remain available for those who are not in need.
This brings me to the question of regional disparities. As I previously mentioned, solving the problem of the poor by taking from the non-poor is temporary and unsatisfactory. The problem must be solved not by taking from the non-poor and giving to the poor but by providing opportunities for the poor so that they, on their own initiative, can become non-poor. Local regional development would
September 19. 1968

The Address-Mr. Pringle lead to increased productivity in that area and the regional disparity would disappear.
Returning to the just society, may I say I feel that a compulsory medicare program, is not just. I am not opposed to medical insurance. I think that medical insurance is good, as is car insurance or fire insurance. However, I am opposed to compulsion because compulsion takes away a man s freedom of choice. When you take away a man's freedom of choice, then you are creating a situation in which there is decreased justice. I know the medicare scheme has already been discussed at length but I should like to see reconsideration of it. I agree there should be a conference between the federal government and the provinces to reassess the scheme as it exists, to provide medical services for the needy but on a voluntary basis for those who are not in need. In my opinion, this would be more just.
These are my comments, Mr. Speaker, on the three major problems facing the constituency of Athabasca today: agriculture, with particular reference to the uneconomic farm unit and wheat sales; poverty and unemployment, with particular reference to the Metis and Indians; and isolation, with particular reference to northern road construction and television services. I hope the government will take up the challenge and face these problems without delay.
