Mr. Speaker, I trust I will be forgiven if I mention the fact that three lovely ladies from Chilliwack, which is some considerable distance from here, have apparently come to this chamber just to hear me make my maiden speech. I rise as a neophyte to participate in the throne speech debate. I am only too pleased to join my colleagues in extending sincere congratulations to you, Mr. Speaker, on your appointment as Speaker of this house. The masterful manner in which you direct deliberations has already indicated that procedures here will be expedited. The province of British Columbia is especially proud that the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) was selected to second the motion for the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne which was so ably moved by the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin).
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
At the outset I wish to pay tribute to my predecessor, Reverend Alex B. Patterson of Abbotsford, B.C. He served my riding with
I Mr. Yewchuk.l

sincerity and desire for almost 18 years, broken only by a four year period from 1958. He was temporarily replaced by a more Conservative friend of mine, Mr. Harold Hicks of Agassiz.
I would also ask your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, to permit me to bring greetings from Mr. George Cruickshank of Abbotsford who was the last member of parliament of the Liberal party to represent my riding. He served the constituency diligently and well.
It appears fitting, Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as my election replaced the acting leader of a political party and the election of the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault) also replaced the leader of a political party, that we now sit as neighbours on the side previously occupied by our predecessors. I assure the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that although we are entrenched here next to the demilitarized zone, we shall at all times endeavour to represent our areas with a proper measure of decorum.
The speech from the throne confirms the pre-election assertions to my constituents-a pragmatic and fresh approach to good government.
My constituency is Fraser Valley East in the lush garden of Canada, British Columbia. By virtue of the comparatively limited space suitable for land farming, my area leans heavily to diversity in food production. The constant increase in urban population is creating new challenges to our farmers. The splendorous mountains serve to attract tourists but also severely limit future food production.
The preservation of green areas in the Fraser Valley has now reached a degree of urgency and is a challenge which must surely be met in the very near future. It is my fervent plea that during this session of parliament we will consider ways to provide leadership by persuading other governments, whether provincial, municipal or civic, to plan now for future land accommodation in the Fraser Valley, so as to meet the food requirements of British Columbia s urban areas and avoid costly transportation of products from east of the Rocky mountains.
The people of my riding view with increasing alarm the serious threat to our farm lands which will certainly result if plans proceed to establish new railway links through these rich lands. Our two national railways, acting in concert with B.C. Hydro, seem determined to impose the Roberts Bank railway line despite the alternative route which exists, a route
September 19, 1968

which has the full support of planning authorities and a host of interested associations. Thousands of acres of fertile cash crop acreage have already fallen prey to industrialists who are unquestionably placing monetary expediency above the present and future requirements of the people. It is the earnest wish of my constituents, as evidenced by the multitude of submissions, that parliament promptly use whatever jurisdictional authority it can muster to revise existing plans based on the findings of the lower mainland regional planning board.
The wise decision of the federal government to assist in distributing cereal feed grains throughout Canada on a reasonably equitable basis has resulted in accelerated development of the production of animal proteins for our daily diet. This segment of the agricultural industry, coupled with small fruits, cole crops, field vegetables and tree nuts, provides adequate supply with surplus to ship to other markets.
Fraser Valley farmers are somewhat puzzled by the recent report from the Economic Council of Canada to the effect that there is a serious gap in agricultural technological advance compared with the United States. Those who have been heavily involved in the production of eggs, poultry meat, dairying, turkey production, cash crops and vegetables simply cannot agree. The degree of continuous technological exchange between the United States and Canada as related to the above segments of the agricultural industry has been great indeed. It has been a two-way street beneficial to farmers in both nations.
It is true that financial resources available for research and development are limited in Canada and this permits our American friends to make more rapid progress. However-and this is my point-we have found no evidence of any attempts to stifle technological exchange. The limiting factors, Mr. Speaker, are population disproportion, disturbing to the Canadian domestic market, plus the variables of volume of production. Technological advances cannot create markets. Conversely, Mr. Speaker, they can aggravate costly surpluses. My constituents have already taken the necessary steps to operate their segments as economic units, acting as procurement commissions to secondary industries. This highly successful approach to marketing has been in operation for many years and operates without benefit of governmental or civil service interference other than
The Address-Mr. Pringle enabling legislation. Their theory is: "Production on a business basis to amply serve available markets with lower cost product controlled by area competition, subject only to necessary governmental ground rules".
My constituents were delighted to learn of the proposed federal marketing legislation announced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson). Our people are looking forward to providing assistance through consultation and planning.
At this date, Mr. Speaker, a serious problem exists within the sphere of turkey production throughout all of Canada. The threat of imports of live and eviscerated turkeys from the United States at laid-down prices which are less than the Canadian cost of production is severely damaging our turkey industry. A close study of the circumstances responsible for this problem indicates that the very future of the Canadian turkey industry is in jeopardy.
The existing inequitable competition created by vertical integration in the United States bears no relation to technological advances. Volume of production and consumer population of 20 to 1, which establishes overall cost quotients, constitute an insurmountable barrier under existing tariff schedules. My constituents are pleased to know the Department of Agriculture now has this intolerable situation under study as a matter of urgency. I am advised by my constituents that the farmers in my area are unanimously agreed that government subsidies should only be established as a last resort.
The Fraser Valley, and especially my constituency of Fraser Valley East, has been threatened with flooding by the mighty Fraser river on a regular basis. Floods which have occurred have been devastating. The recently signed agreement between the government of Canada and the government of the province of British Columbia is indeed a welcome respite. Our constituents are looking forward to phase two as related to water level control in the upper areas and reiterate their request that progress be initiated as soon as economically possible.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I am pleased to report that it is our privilege in Fraser Valley East to have a goodly number of Indian reservations within the area. It has been my privilege to meet with many of the chiefs of those bands and to become acquainted with their earnest desire to become involved officially in participation
.. 1
September 19, 1968

The Address-Mr. Pringle in the planning of the future of Indian communities in Canada. We are proud to be acquainted with Chief William J. Mussell of the Skwah band, a graduate of the University of British Columbia and a leader of community life in Abbotsford, British Columbia. One does not remain long in the company of our Indian friends, when they are in session at their regular meetings, without being convinced that any delay in the rewriting of the Indian Act would indeed be a travesty of justice.
Few areas in Canada south of the Northwest Territories utilize modern aviation to span the inaccessible approaches to remote sections more than the people of British Columbia. Even those areas now served by highways lean heavily on all types of aviation to reduce travel mileage and conserve time. My constituency alone boasts of seven licensed airports. The popularity of aviation is such that one airport, Abbotsford, now hosts the largest air show on the North American continent. A show which started as an air circus many years ago has progressed to where it now serves as the acknowledged market place and air exposition of international aviation. No less than 340,000 visitors attended the three-day show in August, 1968. Among them were many from the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Portugal, South Africa, and the United States. It is my pleasure, Mr. Speaker, to issue an invitation today to all those present within the House of Commons chamber to visit the show in 1969. It will be held in August.
My constituents place great faith in the future of aviation, especially at the general aviation or private flying level. Today's vast Canadian air transport system owes its favourable position to the pioneers who fought with unparalleled tenacity to prove it could be done. The Department of Transport must be highly praised for insistence in the belief that at some point in the past flying was here to stay. It is true that the development of huge aircraft now commanding preference for world travel is phenomenal. However, facts which are sometimes ignored indicate that general aviation and private flying have also advanced at an accelerated rate. It is the earnest hope of those who still pioneer the regional routes and fly privately that apathy relating to private flying will not develop in government to the point where Canadian aviation will be measured by the requirements of the large air transport companies. There is a challenge now for Canadians to

insist that technological advances necessary in the field of air navigation and airports keep step with other nations of the world.
I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, if I failed, even at this date, to mention the impact that Expo '67 has had in stimulating the Canadian tourist trade. Many exciting and rewarding experiences await those who travel the length and breadth of our land. More Canadians than ever are learning about Canada. I know of no better method of promoting Canadian unity than for easterners to travel west and for westerners to travel east. Many new members of the house, including myself, are now determined to learn the other official language, not as a requirement, Mr. Speaker, but as a privilege. It will be my pleasure to endeavour to promote the tourist exchange concept in my area and to extend a sincere invitation to easterners to come on out west and get to know all of your vast, firmly united nation.
Despite our affluent society we confess that there are areas requiring special development, either to initiate progress or replace industry which is being abandoned in the interest of centralization or integration. It is our hope that guidelines to include all unfortunate sections of Canada will emerge from studies of all depressed areas.
The immense challenge involved in establishing a truly just society will require the united efforts of all Canadians, for a just society cannot be established by laws alone. The election demonstrated that Canadians have, with good reason, placed their confidence in our brilliant chief executive officer, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau). His steadfast determination to involve all Canadians in the task of moulding Canada into an even more united and purposeful nation is inspiring this great land as never before.
I am proud to be a member of this parliament. I look forward to serving and working with all the members of the House of Commons. I look forward to participating in the decisions of Canada's twenty eighth parliament which I am sure will be one of the most productive in Canada's history.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I wish to extend my congratulations to you on being appointed Speaker. I am sure that you and the other officers who have been appointed will serve this house in a way we can all be proud of.
Before beginning my general remarks may I say that I was disappointed with several
September 19, 1988
aspects of the throne speech. I wish to mention four or five matters that are pertinent at this time to my constituency. As many hon. members probably know, one of the world's largest potash deposits is to be found near Easterhazy in the southeast part of the riding I represent. It was recently announced by I.M.C., the international mineral people, that they are planning to truck the potash to a point across the United States border for shipment on United States trains to Chicago. If that happens there will be serious economic repercussions to the city of Melville, which is a potash transportation centre at this time. If the transportation facilities are not to be used it will mean that many families in the area will be without jobs. I just wish to bring that to the attention of the house and I hope that it will be possible to avoid bringing about this economic setback to the community in Melville.
I also wish to express my concern about the cancellation of the winter works program, since it affects the cities and towns in my constituency. The cancellation will bring hardship not only for the towns themselves but also for many families. I am sure that as a result unemployment this winter will increase, and I wish to second the remarks of members of the opposition and on the government side who have spoken about this matter.
I also wish to talk briefly about the problems of the Indian Metis people. I have grown up with Indian people. I was raised on a farm which was near a reservation. There are about six Indian reservations in the constituency of Yorkton-Melville, and I would like to congratulate the hon. member who seconded the address in reply for his discussion of Indian problems. It is about time the Indian people had equality with the rest of society. It is about time they were given the right to make more of the decisions affecting their own lives.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The most important issue in the constituency of Yorkton-Melville is, of course, agriculture. First of all I want to say I concur 100 per cent with what was said by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave) in this house a couple of days ago. I think he quite adequately described the pressures facing Saskatchewan farmers today. He talked about the cost-price squeeze and its effect on the farming industry. The time has come when the government must act to alleviate the farmers' problems. We must introduce a
The Address-Mr. Nystrom vigorous campaign to sell wheat internationally. We must do something to raise the price of wheat. I suggest that the farmer receive $2.12 a bushel for all the wheat he sells abroad, and an extra $1 per bushel for wheat used domestically, up to a level of 1,000 bushels per farmer.
Something must be done about the skyrocketing increase in the price of farm machinery. Here I would suggest we begin by establishing a prices review board to investigate the cost of farm machinery. We must extend farm credit and make interest free loans available to young farmers wishing to establish themselves in the industry. Agriculture is the No. 1 industry in the province of Saskatchewan, and indeed is one of the basic industries in all of Canada. It is about time we started to realize this and gave farmers a better deal.
I would now like to introduce something new into the throne speech debate Mr. Speaker. I could go on to talk about many of the problems in my constituency but that is something I will be doing throughout the session. Now, however, I would like to introduce a new topic because it is very important to the government of Canada although it is something politicians, regardless of their political affiliations, do not talk about.
I do this for basically two reasons. First, I do not want to duplicate some of the things members of my party have already said and, second, more importantly it is an issue of very grave concern to this house and the country. I want to talk about young people and how they relate to this chamber and to the political process in Canada and throughout much of the world.
For young people democracy is on trial right here and now. We have heard a lot about alienation, about frustration, student unrest, riots, hippies, yippies, beatniks and similar groups within me youth community. All of these phenomena are important to this house for one reason. That reason is that the verdict on the democratic system by many of these young people has already been made and that verdict is guilty-guilty of irrelevance, guilty of lack of purpose, guilty of lack of meaning for their lives but, most important of all, the political system has been found guilty for its failure to produce results here and now.
I have mentioned alienation. What is alienation? It is the separation of the individual from his activity. Political alienation is the separation of the individual from



September 19, 1968
The Address-Mr. Nystrom what is going on right here in this house. What do I mean by this and how does one recognize this kind of alienation in society?
You can recognize this alienation in many different ways. The first way of recognizing it is by the sheer indifference that many have to the political process. On the one hand we have the drop-outs. I have mentioned the hippies, yippies, beatniks and the like, but on the other hand you have indifference on the part of what one could probably call the average kid, the average student who could not care less about the political process. This is the person who is a product of society's major institutions, the person who year in and year out has had the fact pounded into him that he must submit to authority without question. He has been taught to be indifferent, to be apathetic, to conform, and thus he does not really care what happens in the government of Canada or in the whole political process.
You also recognize alienation in a more articulated manner from many of the young people who have attempted to get involved in the decision-making process and have failed. You find groups of these people all over the world. To mention just a few there are the civil rights movement in the United States, the Viet Nam action committees in Canada, the United States and Europe, and we have student activists around the world.
This kind of activity is now cropping up in high schools. We have had recent instances of it in Montreal and in the province of Newfoundland.
This despair is found in student riots, for example, in France and Czechoslovakia. We can see it in many wildcat strikes breaking out throughout the nation. It is a frustration with the slow process of normal procedures of government.
What does all this mean to those of us who are here in parliament? I think it first means that young people are no longer interested in proving themselves to the political process as it exists. What it does mean is that the political process has to prove itself to them. It means that a government, a political party, and the leaders of political parties have to prove themselves to young people. And if they do not, not only will parliament be powerless in regard to the corporate interests of the country but it will also find itself powerless in terms of its relationship to an ever-increasing portion of society. This is the youth community and let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, that about half Canada's population, or more, is well under the age of 30.

This frustration is a real factor that we have to contend with in society. It appears not only in the youth community but in the slums and ghettos. It is becoming evident in the Metis groups and among the native population, and also among many of the small farmers in western Canada. I could mention various campuses and youth associations, but I will relate just one example which will demonstrate the point I am talking about. This is but one of the many examples where action was taken outside the political structure. Action was taken outside the political process to speed things up and make them more relevant, and it produced results.
The incident I am referring to took place at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia. The faculty and students of the university used to eat together in one huge cafeteria. Then one day some of the senior faculty members decided they wanted a separate eating place for themselves and so they constructed a wall across the cafeteria dividing it in two. The vast majority of the student body did not like this. They objected to the wall being built. They went through the normal political structure on the campus to have the wall removed, but their request got tied up in committee after committee until one night a number of faculty members and a group of students got together and tore the wall down, and the wall stayed down. This is an example of where the normal channels failed and people went outside them to solve the problem.
In many ways this parliament is similar to some of the senior faculty of the university I have just mentioned. This is an institution which is not relevant to many Canadian people. If we do not open our eyes soon many more walls may be torn down by young people, discontented farmers, minority groups and the poor. Parliament and the university are similar institutions in our contemporary society. They are both primarily middle and upper class orientated.
The difference between the two is that there is a growing awareness within the university community. It is becoming aware that education is a right, not a privilege. Members of that community are starting to talk about universal accessibility to education at all levels. They are starting to talk about abolition of student fees, about providing living allowances to students, about expanding university educational facilities and making a university education more relevant to today's society.
Meanwhile, on the other hand parliament, the government and the speech from the throne have all failed even to recognize the
Sepiember 19, 1968

underprivileged and the powerless segments within our society such as the poor, the Indian and the marginal farmer, to mention just a few. If we do not open our eyes to this reality, Mr. Speaker, then many people within the near future will be left with no alternative but to start tearing down some walls of their own. These people are absolutely fed up with the verbal dribble, the fancy cliches and democratic rhetoric stemming from this chamber and that once again is found in the speech from the throne. It is becoming more and more apparent that the government cannot see the forest because of the trees.
I believe it was Rousseau who said, "Since inqualities exist within society it is the duty of legislatures to remove those inequalities." So far parliament is not playing an active role in supporting equality in Canada. If we do not affirm equality, dignity, and the right of people to act meaningfully in their own community, if we do not take some of the practical steps that have been suggested toward these ends, if young people do not get universal accessibility to education, if farmers do not get a two-price system for wheat, if the taxation system is not reformed, and if we do not do something about the ludicrous cost of housing and rocketing increases in rents then parliament will naturally become more irrelevant to people in Canada.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
If the impersonality and power of corporate bureaucracy are not torn down to allow people to participate, then parliament will fade farther into the background of peoples' lives, and they will naturally seek alternative paths of social change. Idealistically, government should be an institution which people can collectively work through to solve the problems which they cannot solve as individuals. As the age of automation increases the sphere of meaningful individual action increasingly contracts.
The need for open participatory institutions in society is becoming more and more a necessity. The basic institution should be government, the people, in other words; but it will never be so long as we are committed to a philosophy of Liberalism which is a philosophy of limited government. The basic philosophy of Liberalism prevents it from attacking private centres of power in society that lie at the root of our country's problems. Instead of control of irresponsible private power the government is deferential toward it.
The Address-Mr. Nystrom
We can see this failure in every segment of our society. I have mentioned a number of aspects. We see it in the taxation system, in the failure to plan the economy and in the failure in any way to grapple with the foreign ownership problem of our economy. Young people and other people as well are starting to ask many very pertinent questions. They are asking where the real roots of power lie in our country. They are starting to ask why the Liberal party, the government, does not release an account of their contributors in the last election campaign. Why will they not do this? It is relatively simple; they will not because then the people would know who have vested interests in the government of Canada. This is one of the major binds on democracy that can be placed clearly on the doorstep of the people sitting across the aisle.
Later I shall be introducing a bill to lower the voting age in Canada from 21 to 18. This is just one important way to open up society for participation. We all know that in the election campaign the Prime Minister invited young people to participate. He said, "Come, and we will participate together in building a greater Canada for all". But then he denied them the basic right of participation, the right to vote. The more one watches the government the more one realizes it is an old man type of government with an old philosophy and reactionary ideas.
We must face up to many problems in our changing world. The government must not act as a deterrent to change. It should be in the forefront of change leading the way. We must eradicate things such as poverty and pollution. We must reform the tax system and we must alleviate the housing crisis. In fact we must set up new objectives and priorities for society. If the government does not soon face up to some of these facts, then the youth image of the Liberal party will become mouldy and musty with age.
I strongly believe that if we open our eyes we can make some of these things more relevant. I have a lot of faith in the democratic system of government. All we have to do is make it more pertinent, more modern and get the people participating.
I should like to conclude my first speech in this chamber by quoting a line often used by the late Senator Robert F. Kennedy just before his untimely assassination a few months ago. He said, "Some men see things as they are and say why; I dream things that never were and say why not."

Mr. Speaker, I would like at the beginning of my remarks to pay the customary respects to the Speaker, and to you also for your recent appointment as Deputy Chairman of the committees of the house. I am convinced that if you follow the example of the Speaker, you will discharge your duties perfectly.
I would like also to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the Throne (Messrs. Corbin and Marchand). Both made interesting speeches and deserve our congratulations.
I also want, Mr. Speaker, to welcome to the house one of my university colleagues, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Gervais) who won his seat in the last election. We have always been a very good friends and, although we have had our political differences, our friendship has never been affected by them. I am therefore very happy to see him in this house.
Mr. Speaker, after a very eventful convention, the Liberal party elected a leader. Knowing the Liberal party as we do, we know that its members took advantage of the circumstances to place less accent on real leadership qualities but more on the candidate's gift for acting. In fact, during the election campaign, our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave good account of himself as such by giving kisses unstintingly and keeping a constant smile. While refusing to deal with the main economic problems facing our country, he nevertheless succeeded in getting great majority.
And as the Conservatives are always magnanimous people, may I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate him on the victory he won in the last election.
We were pleased, Mr. Speaker, to see the Liberal party at long last get an absolute majority in the House of Commons. How often has the official opposition not been accused of slowing down the business of the house, of systematic obstruction, of filibuster. Especially the last Liberal government accused us of so doing, to camouflage its lack of competence in introducing appropriate legislation in the House of Commons.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
This government having been elected with a majority, we hope it will take over the leadership of the house and the honourable members across the floor may rest assured that we, of the Conservative party, are going

to maintain our co-operation with the government in power in order to try and bring about for all Canadians legislation that will be beneficial to our nation.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister had intimated after the election that his government would introduce legislation and a speech from the Throne, both of an extraordinary nature. He went so far as to say that the Conservatives would be amazed. In general, Canadians were expecting that the new Prime Minister and his cabinet were to present some extraordinary legislation which would be spectacular, different, imaginative, that would create an impact on the imagination of all Canadians.
Some political friends of our colleagues opposite who had come to Ottawa with the resolution to applaud the Speech from the Throne went back home extremely disappointed because they found out, as we did, that the Speech from the Throne presented by the government contained nothing but left-overs from the previous Pearson administration, heated up again in a new frying pan by the present Prime Minister.
For this reason, we cannot evidently congratulate the government on its Speech from the Throne, because we feel that it suffers from a lack of vitality and dynamism which the country needs at present to resolve the problems that are facing it.
Evidently, we had thought that this government would be a "new look" government with a new vision. A youthful Prime Minister would obviously stand out the moment the session began, but we have noticed that expressions such as were used during the election campaign have been incorporated in the Speech from the Throne and they were not defined.
During the election campaign, smiling his famous smile, the Prime Minister talked of the just society. He never said exactly what he meant by it. He never adapted the concepts of a just society to the political, economic and social problems facing Canada at the present time.
There is nothing in the Speech from the Throne to illustrate the concept of the just society of which the Prime Minister and his team spoke during the election campaign. In our opinion, therefore, this is again a case of the Liberal party formulating grandiose principles, as it alone does so well, in order to gain votes during an election campaign.
September 19, 1968
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, a government which calls itself modern in 1968 must legislate in order of priority. We have often said so in this house. Even though priorities were mentioned in the Speech from the Throne, the Prime Minister has not told us what priorities he has established. We must examine not only the long-term priorities but also short-term priorities, because indeed we must not be blind. We are up against an alarming unemployment problem, for statistics reveal that 400,000 people without work or looking for work at this time.
We also have a housing problem. In fact, we know that a third of the population in the larger urban centres is still living in slums and that the government has not found a practical solution to try to help those people.
We know also that the cost of living is still extremely high and that women with children have a terribly hard time to make ends meet.
In addition, agriculture is not in a very prosperous state, and when I hear my colleagues talk about the problems of agriculture in the west, I would like them to come to Quebec to see the alarming conditions which prevail in agriculture there.
Although 10,000 farmers from eastern Canada, Quebec and Ontario came last year to beg the Minister of Agriculture to give them better prices for their dairy products, that problem still remains. The other problems submitted by the U.C.F. to the previous government were left unsolved and the present government must have forgotten them since there is not a word about them in the Speech from the Throne. [DOT]
Mr. Speaker, we also know that our economic growth is at a standstill. Our productivity needs to be boosted to make it more profitable and thus give a higher standard of living to all Canadians.
The economy of a country increases through the development of its natural resources, hence the necessity for a government that believes in priorities to advocate and introduce immediately in the house legislation for the establishment of short and long term programs so that our natural resources may be developed in a national way.
Another priority of the government is to introduce legislation and take decisions to increase the number of employment opportunities in our country. We all know that the government also intends to give priority to constitutional reform.

However, the present manpower program did not, in my estimation, produce all the expected results. I observed that in one municipality within my constituency, sixty-year old people were being retrained and made to attend sixth and seventh grades; it made me wonder whether this program truly pursues the intended objectives.

I wish to thank my colleagues for giving me this opportunity to continue my remarks, Mr. Speaker. I shall try to be brief; besides, I think I shall be through in a few minutes.
As I was saying, the constitutional principles set out by the Liberal party and now brought forward in the Speech from the Throne had already been recognized by us during our convention in Toronto.
The right hon. Prime Minister speaks of the constitutional equality of languages. We too referred to it in a resolution, in Toronto. Now, Mr. Speaker, for the sake of the record and to make some Liberal members understand that we are not against national unity, that we are not going to tear apart Canada on constitutional matters, I repeat that we never said that. We never said, when we spoke of two nations, "The two founding people", that this meant two Canadas. We only meant one Canada made up of two large majorities plus other ethnic groups, which of course, would be minorities.

We have said that Canada is and must remain a federal state and that Canada is made up of the two founding nations endowed with historical rights, to which many people coming from a number of countries have joined themselves. We said that the constitution should be drafted so as to allow and promote full and harmonious coexistence, as well as advancement and equality for all Canadians. We have repeated and we even included it in a document drafted and adopted at the Toronto convention that the constitution is a Canadian document which could not be changed anywhere else. Therefore, I fully endorse my leader when he says to the hon. Prime Minister that the very first constitutional step this government should take is to repatriate our constitution so as to allow us to amend it ourselves.
I think that is the first priority from the point of view of the constitution and in that respect I fully agree with the leader of my party. We said also that, in our opinion, it was necessary to create a constitutional tribunal with the power to settle the constitutional problems which could arise between the provinces or between a province and the federal government, or still the problems which the Supreme Court of Canada could refer to it. That is one of the matters that were brought up during the federal-provincial conference on the constitution held here last February. We advocated also in that resolution that the constitutional equality of the French and English languages should be recognized to guarantee French Canadians throughout the country the right to get an education in their own language wherever possible, the use of the French language in the legislatures and before the courts, just as the Englishspeaking residents of Quebec enjoy those rights now. The status of the official languages is precisely what the Prime Minister wants to obtain today. It would mean that, at the constitutional level, we disagree. But it is precisely the constitutional policy, that kind of amendment to the constitution that the present Prime Minister wants to introduce.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have this opportunity to speak in this house. Even though I am almost an old-timer since this is my fourth term here, I still have many things to say, because the past efforts did not yield great results.
I take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate you on your re-election as Speaker. I offer my congratulations also to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne (Messrs. Corbin and Marchand).
I will merely speak of concrete things in this speech, Mr. Speaker. Everyone speaks of a just society and of guaranteed incomes, but nobody ever defined these terms.
Mr. Speaker, I will now attempt to define these main terms. I would like to say to the people and to members of this house what are exactly the problems of our economy, where reforms should be made and where distributive economy should be applied, that is to whom should the benefits-or the products, if you prefer-of our economy go.
First of all, the human being should be protected if every citizen is to have full benefit of a living, active and progressive economy. All these conditions must be fulfilled if priority is to be given to the individual, who has been neglected in the past. Priority is given to finance, to capital, but the human capital is forgotten. Everything is done, nothing is neglected for the money capital, but the most noble, the most important one, the human capital, is neglected. This is what I intend to deal with and demonstrate in my statement.
All Canadians want a united Canada, but they also want a just society. Like everyone, we have been advocating a just society and a united Canada for a long time. That is nothing new.
September 19. 1968

The Address-Mr. Latulippe
The people heard vague words and believed that they were hearing something new. That is one of the reasons why they once again elected the great Liberal party. By the way, I should like to say right away, Mr. Speaker, that we intend to co-operate fully with the party in power and with all who present legislation intended to serve, protect and help the people and allow them to live decently. We will support all good legislation.
However, we will stand against all measures which do not protect the individual or which protect only capital. Naturally, we will oppose all tax increases, because they affect the individual unfavourably and because we are overtaxed already. We will support all good measures which are beneficial to the individual and which give him priority.
It is apparently agreed that we all want to build a united Canada in a just society which undertakes to eliminate provincial and regional inequalities. It is a worthy effort, a good attempt, a noble ambition, but a shared hope. There are inequalities not only in constitutions, but between the provinces, the different public organizations and the various regions.
First, there are inequalities affecting the family. Every individual must be allowed to live decently in his country. Canada is not only made up of more or less prosperous provinces and regions. A united Canada is made up also, and above all, of families enjoying more or less prosperity and of human beings who are more or less prosperous.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
There are persons, families, regions, provinces, institutions, municipalities that are more or less prosperous in a united Canada, within a just society. That is a noble pursuit that does not omit any aspect of the just society, of a united Canada. Canada is made up mainly of these 20,700,000 human beings who are Canadian citizens, made of flesh and bones, each with their own mind who are members of some five million dwellings or families in Canada.
Therefore, it is first on a personal and family basis as well as on a basis of the essential needs of persons and families that an immediate foundation of a just society must be realized and which will result in a united Canada this very year.

Assuredly, the large administrations on the national, provincial, regional, municipal, social and even on the international and world levels are important and deserve our continued attention.
Undoubtedly, all the great institutions were set up with the commendable idea of promoting progress, productivity and growth of economic activity in the interest of the whole community.
Nonetheless, Mr. Speaker, it should be realized, at last, that this is expected by the whole population, that is, our 20,700,000 Canadian citizens living in flesh, bone and spirit, and not only the 7,700,000 adult and productive citizens who are reasonably rewarded for their work or their capital.
Nevertheless, one should understand, in the end, that the whole population includes 13 million dependants, without work nor capital, without personal income, but entitled unquestionably to live among all of us, in a united Canada, according to the 1968 standard of living.
But for all that, it should be realized in the end, once and for all, that the right to live which every citizen without revenue is entitled to must be appraised and determined by a certain amount of money, the same way as a salary is set for any work, or the same way as interests are recognized by contract on any capital loaned or invested under conditions clearly determined between free parties.
So, if the 7,700,000 Canadian citizens contributing to national production receive a fair share proportional to their work or their capital, if, also those 13 million Canadian citizens without work or capital receive each month, in every home, a guaranteed minimum revenue, which constitutes their personal vital right, thus, and thus only, shall we have achieved a just society, a united Canada where every citizen will be happy and proud to live, respected and glorified, in the full view of the whole world filled with amazement.
Even though the right hon. Prime Minister did not make any promises during the last election, he said again and again that the objectives of his administration would be a just society and a united Canada. Those are happy words which were appreciated and which led the Liberal party to the victory. It is up to us now, Mr. Speaker, to convert those words into action, into deeds, into achievements.
September 19, 1968	COMMONS
Each citizen may have his own idea about a just society and a united Canada, but I think everybody would accept a conception whereby each Canadian citizen could share in the prosperity of Canada.
I feel the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the just society and a united Canada envisaged should provide for what I have just pointed out.
It is not, Mr. Speaker, by begging, grumbling or advocating separatism. No one seeks to break away from a group where it gets a fair treatment. In this prosperous Canada, production reached $68 billion in 1968, that is about $3,300 per head or $16,500 per family of five, which is marvelous and satisfactory for the majority of Canadians. There is no reason for allowing such a magnificent production to be so badly distributed among the population of this country. Why, Mr. Speaker, is there so much suffering, so much poverty and insecurity amidst such abundance, so many riches, such a tremendous production? Let us at least work in such a way that the most unfortunate may reach a viable and convenient human condition. It is not poverty, Mr. Speaker, that must be driven away, not poverty against which we must wage war, as many members seem to believe, but injustice. It is fraud, frustration of the rights to live of each Canadian citizen. This must be eradicated.
Poverty in itself does not exist. But injustice exists. Inequities must be replaced by a little more justice. This is the point I want to make, Mr. Speaker. Chapter 44 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1960, well specifies that each Canadian citizen is entitled to life, liberty, security of his person and enjoyment of property whatever may be his race, his national origin, his colour, his religion or his sex.
We are only considering here the right to live of each Canadian citizen who is penniless and unemployed. We are considering the recommandations of the World Charter of Human Rights and of the Canadian Charter of Human Rights passed in 1960. We are only demanding that this right to live be recognized to each Canadian who is penniless or unemployed by allowing him to earn his living as we recognize his right to receive wages and the right to collect a rate of interest on invested capital. Therefore, if in Canada at the present time, our production

That is the crux of of the problem, if it could finally be understood.
It is not a matter of political party, nor of a philosophic system. It is a matter of fraternity, humanity, balanced economy and progressive policy, through unity, justice and goodwill. It is not a matter of race, nationality, religion, language, social classes. It is a matter of dollars, it is the right to live, to have the bare necessities. It is the right of a guaranteed minimum income for all Canadian citizens, 20,700,000 of them, of which 7,700,000 have incomes gained through their capital or their work, and 13 million are dependent on a productive citizen or society in general.
Let us open our eyes to this metaphysical and mathematical reality, capital and work are the two pillars of production, but production is geared to consumption. Now, there are in Canada, in 1968, 7,700,000 productive citizens and 13 million dependants.
There are in this country 7,700,000 citizens, drawing income from their work and capital, and 13 million citizens without any income derived from work or capital, but who all have the right to live in Canada according to the 1968 standard of living in this country. This right to live is a right that must be assessed and paid, as well as the right to give a salary for one's work or the right to draw interest from capital.
In our economic system, we are doing the opposite of what is required. Instead of paying a minimum guaranteed income to the 13 million dependent citizens, we are increasing wages and capital interests, thereby raising still more the cost of living for all citizens, even for the 13 million dependent citizens without work or capital and hence without any income.
In the case of the citizens who are producing through their work and capital, incomes increase while in the case of the dependent citizens, the expenditures are going up. The
7,700,000	producing citizens are taking advantage of an unbalanced economy while the dependent citizens and their dependants have to put up with this same unbalanced economy.
Here, I am convinced of bringing a logical and practical solution that can be applied immediately in the present and regular mechanisms of our Canadian monetary, economical and political systems of free enterprise,
[Mr. Latulippe.1
whether they are orthodox or capitalist. Why is no attention ever given to this problem? Why must I always speak in this desert? Perhaps I may hope that this desert will at last become a blossoming garden, not only for labour and management, but for all those without work or money and for all the needy who want a just society and a united country.
However, this unity can only be based on individuals and not on groups, companies, regions, provinces, towns or villages.
Canada is 20,700,000 people, and that is the basis on which we must establish a guaranteed minimum income, either through work, or capital, or the vital right of people without work or capital.
Why can the members of this house and this parliament not accept this suggestion immediately? That is why I say to them: Dear colleagues, in every one of your ridings, you saw them during the election campaigns, you saw citizens who have money, citizens who have work, and other citizens who have neither work nor money, who are dependent and without income, because they are too young, too sick, too old, too unfortunate, in short, for all kinds of reasons; you have even seen mothers who stay home and have neither income nor salary for the work they do as mothers and housekeepers.
Have you thought of that? In every home in Canada, to each citizen without work or money, we could distribute a guaranteed income of $1 per day per child, of $2 per day per teenager, of $3 per adult and of $4 per older citizen of 60 and more; have you ever considered how this could solve all personal and family problems in the field of daily finance?
That would be the end of hardship, poverty and insecurity. There would still be good and human poverty, sickness, accidents, occasional misfortunes, curable bad administration, but we would be through with hardship, poverty, insecurity in the normal and wholesome families of our hard-working, honest population which is willing to do the utmost in community life.
And do you know what all that would cost? It would cost 14 per cent of the value of the national production. Do you know that a single program could replace every one of the 200 costly plans administered under social welfare, that are a disgrace because of the famous inquiries which ruin the dignity and the respect of the human being and the private life of individuals and families?
September 19, 1968	COMMONS
Moreover, do you know that by so doing, society, Canada, and we here in this house, would together have done nothing more than something just towards human beings? Because the right to life, to the vital minimum, the individual minimum is not an optional charity, but a real right, a binding right according to justice, based on nature, on natural resources, on the divine fatherhood and on the rights of universal humanity.
During the Speech from the Throne, I was pleased to hear our gracious governor general utter the last phrases:
May Divine Providence guide you in your deliberations.
Could he not have added on the same tone: "and submit you to the sweet rigours of his divine chastisement".
For, in truth, we deserve chastisement. We can no longer let everyone lack the necessities of life in the face of the categorical statements of the most serious representatives of our political economy, the experts of our Economic Council of Canada. It is not up to me to start rewriting that instructive and well-documented volume. But it is my duty to draw attention to a practical solution which would abolish at least misery, poverty, insecurity in all homes in which live the 20,700,000 citizens of Canada, counted one by one, each of whom would always be assured of the necessary minimum income through his work, his capital or his own right.

Out of that production a surplus of $28 billion in profits was reinvested by a small number of citizens who already have more than they need.

Our federal government, our governor in council, to use the expression used by the 23 ministers have the legislative power to raise family allowances immediately to one dollar a day at least instead of the present 20 cents per day, which does not even pay for a quart of milk now. One is surprised at such a statement. All of it is written in the law, Chap. 109 of the Revised Statutes of Canada on family allowances. A similar gesture was made along this line in 1957 by the Conservative government at that time, just before a federal election, for which he was rewarded with the biggest majority since confederation. Does the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) remember it? Has he regretted such an initiative? Why has he not repeated it more often? He is ashamed to tell us. The Governor in Council may make regulations to give effect and to carry out the objects of this Act,
Consequently, at the present time and according to the present legislation of family allowances, the governor in council, that is the 29 ministers of the present legislature elected by the people of Canada and according to the laws voted by the 264 members of

Mr. Speaker, in the first place allow me to tell you that I am quite proud and honoured of having the privilege to take part in the proceedings of the house.
Having witnessed last week the tokens of admiration and esteem which you have received from all those who not only have many years of experience, but also hold

The Address-Mr. Jerome key posts within their party or the government, I take the liberty of telling you, on behalf of all the new members, and I am sure they will not begrudge me, that you can be rightly proud of all those praises. I wish to add right away my congratulations to those which you have already received.
I also want to join all those who congratulated the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin) and the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand). Both stirred our enthusiasm by their brilliant first steps on the parliamentary scene, the first by moving the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne and the other by seconding it. But it is also important to emphasize that they have opened the way for a great majority of us who are new here.

I am very conscious and proud of being a member of this august chamber, and particularly proud to be one of the unusual number of new members in this new parliament. All of us I am sure approached this career with high expectations as to the possibilities of participating in this very vital and important work, and with a full knowledge of the sacrifices this life might entail. But whatever those sacrifices, I am sure all hon. members, particularly the new ones, are most eager to participate in the affairs of our country to the fullest possible extent. So, with these expectations and with the willingness to make the necessary sacrifices, we come to this chamber to see for the first time the manner in which this very important business is conducted.
What a tragic disappointment it was when we witnessed the performance of those who led the attack from the opposition side of the house in this throne speech debate. How disappointing it was to hear the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) who appeared to be preoccupied with a small number of appointments made by the government to positions in the government service. I suppose that was an invitation to us to review the record of that great province of Nova Scotia, of which for so long he was such a capable administrator. Undoubtedly there was the implication that we would not find such a thing had ever occurred during his term of office.
In my view this is not just something to gloss over, something to be hidden under the rug, as though like a small child this government had been caught with its hands in a cookie jar. It seems much more important to
242	COMMONS DEBATES	September 19, 1968
The Address-Mr. Jerome me that we should face with reality the situation which I, as a member of this house and a novice in political life, intend to do.
It would seem that in filling positions in the government service this or any other government should have the opportunity, when choosing between persons of equal capability, to give some consideration to those who have come forward and made some sacrifices in public life. If there is any dishonour in this, then I think all of us have a very disillusioned view of what this life entails, and the very worth-while work involved here.
I was also disappointed to hear the Leader of the Opposition clinging so closely to a program that was introduced only a few years ago, concurrently I suppose with the term of office of a Conservative government. I refer to the winter works program. Most persons to whom I spoke before coming here applauded the decision of the government, a decision which on the face of it was bound to be unpopular with many municipalities. Nevertheless many of the leaders in the municipalities whom I heard being interviewed, and whose comments were reported in the press, said that although this decision upset some of their planned programs, the winter works program had failed and was not doing the job it was designed to do. In the interests of governmental policy to cut-back in spending, this was a courageous and forthright decision for the government to have taken at this time.
It is encouraging to know that this government is prepared to do this kind of thing. What particularly troubled me was the constant reference, not only in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition but in others to which I will refer in a moment, to the absence of government activity in the field of housing and the absence of a reference in the speech from the throne to this very important and vital program. They would appear to be suggesting that they have no knowledge of the very active and vital work of the task force which is going on at the present time, and which is dedicated to that very program. It would seem that they are not aware that in this very city at this moment the task force is at work over in the west block. It would appear also that they are ignoring the calibre of the people who are serving voluntarily on that task force. It would serve no purpose to mention them by name now, except to say that if anyone on the opposition bench had taken the trouble to examine the names of the people serving there, the work that the government is doing would be obvious. That task force is hard at work and began its work

as soon as possible after this government came into office. It has received many briefs from all parts of the country, and has a full schedule laid out for the three forthcoming months. Its program is an ambitious one, indeed.
I should like now to refer to the speech of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) who followed the Leader of the Opposition. If this performance was not as great a disappointment to a new member, it would be from the standpoint of theatrics. The remarks of that hon. gentleman were delivered in perhaps a little more flowery language, with more pathos and tragedy, and more prosaic beauty, but they did not contain any more substance, or an appreciation of the basic nature and value contained in the speech from the throne. It is no wonder that in his remarks the hon. member for York South confronted the Prime Minister with a Shakespearean idiom. It was a theatrical performance at best, full of sound and fury. To carry the quotation further, it was full of sound and fury but signified nothing. That was the most disastrous thing about it all, except for his reference to the situations in Biafra and Nigeria. He spoke as if this government did not concern itself about these problems and was not aware of the grief, tragedy and starvation of these millions of people. From his observations one would be led to believe that this government was not aware of the genocide being permitted day by day, by red tape if nothing else, in many places of the world,- something we are powerless to do anything about.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
What was particularly disappointing is that we waited throughout this diatribe to hear what it is that this government should be doing, what program, action or positive step the government should take, as suggested by the hon. member. In order to demonstrate the terrible default of this government we were finally greeted with precisely the proposal that the federal government of Nigeria has refused to agree to a second air strip. He then said that surely the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) ought to know that Sweden has agreed to lend a plane to the International Red Cross, and if that was the case why did not Canada do the same. After all this diatribe, this was the positive proposal put forward by the hon. member, in his effort to demonstrate the inadequacy of the government in this regard. This situation was covered, however, by the Secretary of State
September 19, 1968	COMMONS
for External Affairs, who said that everything was being done by the Red Cross that could possibly be done and that when more could be done by Canada we would be prepared to assist. Obviously by his remarks the hon. member for York South has wasted the time of the house. He spent several minutes on a foreign affairs peroration having no substance whatsoever.
The only leader on the opposition side of the floor who did not fail to disappoint us was the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette). With his good humour and his wild, fiery style he is never disappointing. Unfortunately, as I listened closely to his remarks, it seemed to me that, flowery as they were, and delivered with such good humour, they were irrelevant to the speech from the throne.
I am sure that I can find agreement among all new members on both sides of the house when I say that the common tragedy of this debate has been the failure of hon. members to recognize the fundamental character of the speech from the throne, having due regard for the majority position in which this government finds itself. For longer than we care to remember this country has experienced and has suffered from the dilemma of minority governments. One member of the N.D.P., against whom I campaigned, continually suggested that he preferred a minority government, that he espoused a government with a minority. I suppose the logical conclusion is that it is only in this situation that this party could acquire this artificial power it has never been given by the electorate.
Notwithstanding the espousal by the hon. member for the N.D.P., we all realize that this neglected country gave a clear mandate to the government. On June 25 of this year the electorate of Canada helped the Prime Minister to gain the success he deserved. They elected a sufficient number of members to allow him to sit in this house with a majority, and to carry on a program of work not only day by day or week by week, and surely not at the will or pleasure of the opposition, but for a period of some four or five years.
How fitting it is that the speech from the throne should outline the philosophy of the government and the programs it intends to carry forward. In this way it demonstrates the fundamental character of the programs that have been planned. It will allow time to plan the use of human resources, time to develop programs through research, time for study and active investigation by the capable

The Address-Mr. Jerome committees of this house, and at the same time it introduces as a matter of urgent priority proposals for parliamentary reform. How appropriate it is that this reform and these far-reaching programs should be concomitant. This will allow parliament to receive and fully consider these programs in the months and years ahead. These are not day to day programs, and in none of the speeches I have heard or read by hon. members have I seen any recognition of this basic fact, or any understanding of these constitutional reforms. The subjects to be dealt with include matters of unity both in a personal and urbane sense, matters of justice and the Criminal Code, problems of industrial relations and disputes, and the system of continuous reporting on prices and costs.
There has been some reference to population expansion and the difficulties caused by urbanization. There has been reference to foreign affairs, including Viet Nam, Biafra and Czechoslovakia. All of these situations and conditions are a challenge to democracy. The programs that have been referred to will expedite our way of doing things and make it possible for us to keep pace with the times.
The challenge put forward in the speech from the throne relates precisely to the shaping up and sharpening up of procedures, so that we can be on time and in pace with the vast volume of legislation and work of this house that is now required to meet the growing needs of our great country. It is for this reason that I suggest those from the opposition who have spoken have failed to understand and appreciate the basic character of the speech from the throne.
Let me hasten to add my support to those who have spoken in support of the address in reply moved by that hon. gentleman on this side of the house, the hon. member for Mada-waska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin), and seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand).
In addition to these general remarks about the speech from the throne I understand it is a traditional privilege given to new members of this house to say something about the beauties of their particular ridings, for the benefit of those hon. members who have not had the opportunity to visit them personally.
The riding of Sudbury is made up mainly of the city of Sudbury and the town of Copper Cliff. We have many beautiful lakes and wooded areas. We have a beautiful new university and a beautiful park which surrounds the one lake in the city. When describing the beauty of that city I must admit sadly that a
September 19, 1968

The Address-Mr. Jerome
great deal of the beauty is to be found in the people themselves, rather than in its physical characteristics. The reason I say that is that we have stood by and witnessed an ineffective program by the provincial government regarding the problem of air and water pollution, much of which is the result of the mining and smelting operations in the Sudbury riding.
One looks at the agricultural potential and the beauty of the area surrounding the city of Sudbury, and then, in a sense of pity, observes the devastation which has occurred to the natural beauty of that area as a result of smoke and gas emitted from the stacks of the smelters. What has been permitted over the years has allowed the mining operations to pollute the air and the waters, so that the grazing lands have been literally destroyed beyond all possible imagination. This has destroyed the beauty of the area and has done away with any possibility of agricultural endeavour. The area is no longer very beautiful, and this is no longer a very scenic city.
Either by constitution or by tradition, this area has been left to the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial government, and its programs have been ineffective. The only guide lines or criteria of those programs have been directed toward the removal of the noxious sulphur content of the gases emitted by the smelter. But these efforts have been linked to guide lines which suggest that, as long as a smelter is economic, and as long as it has been able to provide for the removal of gas, it has been allowed to operate. As long as these companies have been able to make money, or in some cases even break even, the company has overlooked the pollution that occurs, and the noxious gases have been removed only to the minimum required for a profitable operation.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Surely, Mr. Speaker, there must be an area here for this government. Surely it is now time that the federal government moved into this field. We enjoy rights in this area, certainly, under health and welfare, certainly under agriculture, mines, energy and resources. We have clear precedent for authority in this area to get in and work, if not exclusively in this field then in co-operation with the provinces. I know that some legislation is intended, but I urge this government to look very closely at the problems of air and water pollution that exist in the riding of Sudbury which I represent.
It is easy for me to stand here and in my description of these problems condemn the

companies that mine the ore and smelt it there, to condemn the companies associated with them in removing these noxious gases, or attempting to remove them partially only, to the extent that they are able to sell on the market the products gained thereby. But it is not quite as simple as that, for this is not the only area of our country that we leave to the industries, to be guided by economic necessities or economic advantage. A company is entitled to carry on its business for a profit. That is basic to the free enterprise system. Nor is it our function, or my proposal, that the government should be controlling the operations of companies to change that motivation or to in any way diminish the existence or the strengthening of the free enterprise system. But where the legitimate interests of two parties or two groups meet or are in conflict, where it is in the legitimate interest of the company to work its mines for a profit, at the same time it is surely in the legitimate interest of the citizens to be protected from these noxious gases wherever posible. Surely, Mr. Speaker, in order to fill that area in between there is a role for government.
If the provincial government were occupying that role and carrying it out to the fullest of its ability, that might be well and good. In fact, the tragic experience in my riding -which is what I am particularly concerned about-is that this has not taken place. I understand, from speaking with other members who are faced with the same problem, not only in the mining industry but in other industries as well, that they have had similar experiences in other provinces throughout the country. This all the more emphasizes the fact that the time is now for the federal government to move into this field with force, energy and vigour, to do the kind of things that the provincial governments have failed to do.
So in closing, Mr. Speaker, I would plead with this government to look into the problems of this vast pollution and contamination of the air we breathe and the water we enjoy, for the pleasures and for the necessities of life, because even as we stand here, at this very moment the expansion program taking place in the mines of International Nickel Company and Falconbridge Nickel Mines means that the operation is being carried on in such a way as to further prejudice the clear water and clean air that Sudburians are entitled to enjoy. So, Mr. Speaker, this contamination is taking place and is continuing. This government, I plead, should give urgent prior'tv to this problem and see to it that

where the provinces have failed, the federal government can succeed.

Mr. Speaker, first of all let me extend my congratulations to you and to your deputy on the appointment to the positions of Speaker and Deputy Speaker respectively. I feel that the events to date have more than justified the wisdom of the selection of the presiding members of this house. I should also like to express a word of congratulation to the hon. members who have taken part in the debate to date, and to say without fear of contradiction or qualification that the calibre of the debate in this house is worthy of the trust which has been placed in the representatives of the various constituencies throughout Canada.
I should also like to express my appreciation of and to offer congratulations to a former member of this house and a member of the cabinet of the previous administration, who was my opponent during the recent election and also my predecessor, for the great contribution he has made to the house and upon his recent appointment, of which most hon. members are aware. I am referring of course to Hon. Charles R. Granger.

Without the will to settle, all the legislation in the world is useless, and the will to settle is a responsibility that lies just as heavily upon the shoulders of labour as it does on the shoulders of management.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that this week there has been a lot of talk about poverty. I am sure that concern for the poor people of Canada is not the exclusive domain of the Liberal party. Knowing so many people in this house, as I do, I am sure all of us are concerned about poverty and how to solve the problem of poverty. I think we are all agreed it will not be solved overnight, but I think one of the keys to its solution is the need to increase productivity, and increased productivity in this country depends on good will and co-operation between management and labour. That is what we should be working towards in this country. The day has long gone by when management can consider labour as a necessary evil and labour can consider management as something intolerable, an attitude still too prevalent in this country.
I think that possibly the problem of labour unrest in this country is not one solely for the domain of the economists. I think it should also concern our social scientists, sociologists and psychologists. There should be some forces, some people who can understand and reach labour and management and make both parties understand the value of communication. Both parties must understand that the prosperity of this great country depends on the productivity of our secondary industries; and productivity I repeat, depends on cooperation between management and labour, and a mutual respect for each other's particular problems.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Until we achieve that type of productivity, so that we can take advantage of the Kennedy round and the export markets around the world, and are in a position to compete successfully with other countries of the world, then we can talk about the just society for the next 50 years. Labour has a responsible role to play on behalf of the people who are not unionized. Seventy per cent of the labour force has no official spokesman. Who

September 19, 1968

speaks for them in this house? These people have a right to share in the free society. Organized labour has a moral obligation to these people. It has an obligation to co-operate with management just as management has a moral obligation not to treat workers as slaves. Government, labour and management can increase productivity and make the just society possible.
