speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the leader of the Senate, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEach-en) and many others who have helped me become elected to this house. I could not see how I would be elected until these people arrived in my constituency.
I am quite proud to represent the people of southwestern Nova Scotia in the House of Commons. I say this because it is a difficult constituency to represent. It is difficult because all problems exist in my constituency. We have the problem of disparity, housing, poverty, welfare and transportation. The fishing industry faces immediate problems, and many more. It is difficult also from a geographical standpoint because Nova Scotia is barely latched on to the rest of Canada. In addition I represent the southwestern tip of Nova Scotia. Due to this fact the governments seem to forget that people exist there. It is difficult from a racial standpoint because in southwestern Nova Scotia there exist-and I say "exist" because many are not living but merely existing-people of many races. As well as white English speaking people we have Acadians of French descent, we have many people of the Negro race and also a few Indian bands.
Yes, amid difficulties, people exist there. However, when asked by my constituents what I should do in respect of the disparity, poverty and other problems I have simply answered, "The just society will take care of that; don't worry, you will get your share." I hope that my statement will be justified. I hope that the fishermen of Nova Scotia will obtain the same prices for their catch as are obtained by the fishermen of British Columbia. I hope that the people who have emigrated to other parts of Canada will be able to return home to enjoy the same standard of living in southwestern Nova Scotia as is enjoyed by the people of Ontario and other parts of Canada. I hope that the just society will provide for the young people of Nova Scotia a place where they can remain.
The Address-Mr. Comeau
We are not asking for handouts. However, we do desire long term planning with regard to the many problems which face the Atlantic area, particularly Nova Scotia and southwestern Nova Scotia. We require immediate solutions to our problems. We require an immediate solution to the problems affecting our fishing industry. The government has been warned that the fishing industry of Nova Scotia is in the midst of the longest slump ever, with warnings that it could collapse within two years. The chairman of the Western Nova Scotia Fish Packers Association has announced that only Ottawa can come to the rescue, that only Ottawa can relieve the problem. We read in the press that the fisheries ministry has no pat solution to these present problems. Six processing firms have been driven out of the market this year. Over 10,000 residents on the southwestern shore of Nova Scotia will be forced to leave the area. I hope that the organization which is projecting the just society will act soon. Otherwise, as one gentleman said, "We will all have to move out." We are looking for immediate solutions. In addition we are looking for long term planning of the fisheries problem.
The Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Jamieson) while in Nova Scotia on September 3 of this year said that planning is essential to ensure that a decent life, as well as good jobs, is offered to all. Planning is also essential in the field of public works. We are not asking that every village have a new wharf or breakwater. We are asking simply that there be planning so that we will be able to develop good deep water harbours, while maintaining and preserving the present wharves and breakwaters which are already in existence. We ask that the just society distribute evenly the funds available for public works.
There has been planning in the field of transportation. There has been planning for almost 20 years in relation to a Digby-Saint John ferry. I anticipate that soon this will be a reality. But we do not want 20 years of planning. The Prime Minister knows something about our transportation problems because he was fogged down in Yarmouth. At one Liberal campaign meeting Senator McLean stressed the need for improved transportation facilities, larger wharves and more adequate harbour facilities. I hope this statement will be honoured.
I hope that the new department of regional development will formulate some plan to benefit our region. As a result of the discontinuance of the shipbuilding subsidies the
254	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Orlikow shipyards have closed and there has been heavy unemployment. It is our hope that the just society will provide alternative employment for these people, so that they will not find it necessary to go to Chicago, Ontario or elsewhere in order to find employment. Many of my constituents at the present time are not in a wage bracket that enables them to build homes under the National Housing Act. I ask the just society to remedy this situation.

I also ask that the just society fight for the rights of the French minority in Nova Scotia, the district I am representing.
I call Acadians in Nova Scotia second class citizens, because we cannot write or speak properly, either in French or in English, the two official languages of Canada. We must correct this situation with the help of French television and other means recommended by the B. and B. commission. Let us be fair when we distribute funds to the Acadians of Nova Scotia.

The government should not be afraid to get things done in southwestern Nova Scotia, because if four years from now I lose my seat in the House of Commons because things have been done in my constituency I will be proud that I have had some part in this.
I could continue, but I believe this is sufficient to convince the government that the people of the Atlantic provinces, and particularly the people of southwestern Nova Scotia are facing difficult times because of the lack of plans and foresight. I could talk about the harbours from Parkers Cove to Clyde River. I could enumerate the needs. I could go on to talk about a second ferry from Yarmouth to another American port. I could go on and talk about the many studies and inquiries that have been made in southwestern Nova Scotia without any action being taken, but I will leave my comments until later occasions when the ministers concerned are in thier seats. I doubt very much that they will read my comments in any event.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I want to emphasize in respect of this just society that we need action. I will support any government move to uplift the standard of living in the Atlantic area and particularly in southwestern Nova Scotia through any ARDA or regional development agency.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin, as almost
[Mr. Comeau.l
DEBATES	September 19, 1968
every other member who has participated in this debate has done, by congratulating you on your re-election as the presiding officer in this house. A democratic system can only work if the people in the country, whether they are the majority or the minority, have the right to express their views. A democratic government can only work if the members elected, whether they be in the majority or the minority, have the right to express their views and have the feeling that they will be treated with fairness whether they sit on the opposition or the government side.
The years that I have been here since 1962 have been hard years, and they have not been easy years for the Speakers of the house, because they have been years _ of minority government. I am sure that the view I now express is that of every member, and certainly of every member who has been here during previous sessions, that the work of the House of Commons has been made a great deal easier as a result of the fairness, the wit, the humour and charm with which you have handled the difficult task you have been given.
We have heard a good deal in the past months about the just society. The people of Canada were told during the election campaign that one thing this government would do if it was re-elected was move toward a just society. There is reference in the throne speech on several occasions to the just society. However we were given little detail in the throne speech, or in the speech of the Prime Minister the other day, about what a just society means and how it will be implemented. We were given about as much detail as the people of Canada were given during the election campaign. In fact we were told, as were the people of Canada, that there was no need to worry about what a just society meant. We were told that we did not need to understand it or know the details of it, but that all we had to do was trust the Prime Minister. He said that in God's good time, and some of us wondered just who God was, in that sense, we would get a just society. We are still waiting.
I agree with those newspaper columnists who still have great admiration for the Prime Minister and who say that we cannot do everything in one year. Speaking for a great many people, not only members of this house, we would like to see a beginning made on a new, exciting and just society. We would like to see a beginning to the creation of a more equitable Canada of the kind we were led to
September 19, 1968

believe we would begin to see if this government was re-elected. We have yet to see any signs of that.
Indeed, when you try to get anything specific from this government, you receive nothing but empty phrases. It is a common thing in this year 1968 for Canadians, whether they be politicians, university professors, newspaper columnists or ordinary citizens, to look at television, read newspapers and magazines and listen to the radio to learn about what is going on in the United States. We feel that we are quite a bit better off than those people. We are not directly involved in the war in Viet Nam, which many people in Canada believe to be an unjustified war. We do not have the race problems that exist in the United States, or at least we do not admit to them.
It is my belief that we are almost unanimous in our contempt for President Johnson. Last week when the Chrysler Corporation of the United States announced a price increase on the 1969 models, President Johnson, the one for whom a good many of us have a good deal of contempt, did not hesitate to condemn that action of the Chrysler Corporation. I am sure that General Motors and the Ford company will soon follow suit, at which time President Johnson will no doubt take issue with those automobile companies, too. The late President Kennedy not only condemned United States steel companies for increasing their prices, but forced them to rescind those price increases.
We have experienced increases in the prices of some very important and basic commodities within the last year or so. Some months ago we had an increase of about 15 per cent in the price of copper. This was brought to the attention of the government and it was pointed out that the copper companies, Noranda, Hudson Bay Mining and Smelting, and International Nickel, had never made a larger profit than they had during the last year, and that there was no need for that increase in price. It was pointed out that the price of copper was increased because there was a shortage at the time. This government did nothing about that increase.
Last week when Chrysler Corporation announced its intention to increase its prices, members of this chamber asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) if he would intercede. Today the Prime Minister was asked whether he would intercede. What did the Prime Minister say today? He said: "Well, what can I do?" The Prime Minister could certainly do as much as the president of 29180-171
The Address-Mr. Orlikow the United States. He could at least express on behalf of the people of Canada their contempt and their regret that a company such as the Chrysler Corporation, as well as companies such as General Motors and Ford, who will undoubtedly follow suit in the next week or so, would increase prices at a time when their profits have never been as large.
Several years ago the government of Canada, formed by this same government party, made an agreement with the government of the United States under which the tariffs which had been collected on imported automobiles from the United States would be waived by the Canadian government. It was agreed that the $50 million savings in excise tax would go to the companies in order to establish a system under which there would be virtually free trade between the United States and Canada in automobiles. It was felt this would allow these companies to become more efficient, produce more cars at a lower cost and that the prices of automobiles would be reduced in Canada.
It has been said for many years that the reason cars have cost more in Canada than in the United States was the result of our industry being smaller, with smaller production runs, and that it cost more per unit to produce a car here than in the United States.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It was said, when the auto pact was implemented, that we would become more efficient and would not have to produce hundreds of types of models in Canada; that we would concentrate on half a dozen or a dozen models, would produce more cars in Canada, would not have to import them from the United States, and this would bring down the price of automobiles. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) tried to argue today, first of all, that the differential between United States prices and prices in Canada had been reduced since the pact was brought into effect. There is not a word of truth in that statement.
I have here some figures which were prepared by the united automobile workers, the union which I believe represents 99 per cent of the automobile workers in Canada. These figures show what has happened to automobile prices in Canada, as compared to those in the United States, in the years since 1964 when the tax was implemented. In 1964 a six cylinder, four-door sedan produced in Canada had a suggested retail price in this country- and these figures are in U.S. dollars, so that members of the house will understand that the comparisons are correct-of $2,569. In the
256	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Orlikow United States the same ear sold for $2,338, a difference of $231. The price in Canada was 9.9 per cent higher than in the United States.
The price in Canada for a 1965 model of the same car was $2,581. The price in the United States was only $2,350. There was the same difference in price, namely $231 and 9.8 per cent. In 1966 we had the same difference in price. In 1967 the difference in price was reduced by one half per cent. We were still paying 9.4 per cent more in Canada than they were in the United States. This year, the last year for which we have prices, the cost in Canada for this car was $2,727. The same car cost in the United States $2,501. The difference was still 9 per cent, that is, we were paying 9 per cent more for cars selling in Canada than they were in the United States, even though we have a free market.
It has been said, and not denied, that cars produced by the Ford Company in Oakville and sold in Toronto cost more than the same cars produced in Oakville, exported to Buffalo and sold in that city. If this is true- and I know it is-we can assume either one of two things, that the Ford Motor Company is losing money on every car it sells in Buffalo, which I do not think any member of this house would believe for one moment, or the profit for every car sold in the city of Toronto by the Ford Company is exorbitant. Yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce simply waves this fact aside and refuses to do anything, as does the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
We are not talking about some poor fisherman in Newfoundland. We are not talking about some poor farmer in the interlake area of Manitoba. We are talking about some of the largest corporations in the world. General Motors has assets of over $10 billion. The Ford Motor Company has assets of over $5 billion. Chrysler Corporation has assets of over $2 billion. Are the Big Three automobile firms in financial difficulties? Are they not making adequate profits? Do they need this price increase? These are difficult questions to answer precisely because this government, which believes in a just society, has never taken the trouble to enact the most elementary legislation which would require the automobile and other companies operating in Canada, both Canadian and foreign owned, to publish financial statements showing their assets, the extent of their sales and what their profits are. Therefore we cannot be exact in regard to the figures of these companies but some very interesting, and I think pretty accurate, estimates have been made.
[Mr. Orlikow.)
DEBATES	September 19, 19S8
An article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of January 19, 1965, said in part as follows:
According to one estimate, the average annual profit of the auto manufacturers often has run to around 30 per cent of their net worth, that is the total amount of their invested capital compared with a more normal 10 to 15 per cent return in other industries.
While the balance sheets of most of the major producers are closed to public scrutiny, one federal official estimated that in a good year the profit earned by one of the leading Canadian auto producers might run as high as 80 to 90 per cent of invested capital.
This is the kind of company about which the Prime Minister said today he could not do anything. I want to compare that in a moment with the kind of thing the Prime Minister said recently in connection with a group of workers who had the temerity to go on strike, something they had the legal right to do. We do know that in 1967 Chrysler of Canada made a profit, after taxes, of $27,797,000. We do know that the Ford Motor Company of Canada increased its profit between 1966 and 1967 from $16,781,000 to $31,580,000. In other words, Ford Motor Company practically doubled its profit in Canada between 1966 and 1967. Yet we are now being told that despite these very high profits the Chrysler Corporation-and I am sure that in the next few days Ford and General Motors will be doing the same thing-will be increasing the price of 1969 automobiles.
I make these criticisms of the government because I do not believe the government cannot do anything about automobile prices. Of course, Mr. Speaker, the government cannot order the automobile companies to hold the line on prices. Of course, the government cannot, or will not, institute price controls for automobiles. They certainly cannot do this if they are not going to institute price controls on everything else. But there are a number of steps which a government which believes in a just society could take. I wish to list just four steps which the government could take.
First of all, I think the government could, and should, protest publicly the price increases announced by Chrysler and the increases which I am certain will be announced in the next few days by Ford and General Motors. Surely the Prime Minister of Canada, who believes in and has spoken so often and so eloquently outside this house about the just society, can do at least as much as President Johnson of the United States.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Second, the government can, if it believes that the automobile companies of Canada are
September 19, 1968	COMMONS DEBATES
charging too much for their cars in this country, remove the tariffs on the importation of cars. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) gives just the answer I would expect from him; he shakes his head that they cannot do it. Of course they can do it. They can remove the tariffs so that if I, a Canadian citizen, want to buy a car and I am being overcharged, as I know I am, I can go to the United States and buy the same car, thereby saving a substantial amount of money. If the government did that, the Canadian car companies would bring their prices down and thus their prices would become competitive.
Third, the government can order an investigation into the operations of the automobile manufacturers by the anti-combines division so we could get a look at what is actually happening in that industry. Are they really making net profits of 40 per cent or more, as has been alleged by informed observers of the automobile industry, a net profit which is exorbitant?
Fourth, the government should, in the very near future, enact legislation requiring companies, including the automobile companies, to publish financial statements showing their profits year by year, so that the public could judge whether or not the profits of the companies, and therefore their prices, are exorbitant.
These are some of the things which the government could do, and I would urge them to do it. When the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) have been asked in the past few days what action if any they will take, they have made it very clear that they have no intention of taking any action. Indeed the Prime Minister indicated today that there is no action which he could take. I find it strange that the Prime Minister, who believes in the just society and who cannot take any action to control the exorbitant profits of the automobile companies, can hold press conferences at which he lectures workers and tells them to be sensible, reasonable and patriotic, that they should not rock the boat and that they should not ask for exorbitant wage increases, which the Prime Minister implies they are doing.
I should like to quote a couple of sentences from two articles written by George Bain of the Globe and Mail published on July 17 and 18 in which he quoted extensively from a transcript of a press conference given by the Prime Minister. I should like to ask the mem-
The Address-Mr. Orlikow bers of this house to compare the Prime Minister's attitude when he spoke about the postal workers with that which he took today when he was asked to do something about automobile corporations and their exorbitant demands for an increase in the price of cars. This is what he said when he was asked about the strike and about the demands of the workers:
You know that government is the only employer who can meet any wage demands, no matter how high or how preposterous they be, because the government.. . has no money of its own. It just takes money from the taxpayer, whereas in the private sector there is a rock-bottom ... beyond which the employer cannot go because if he gives more he ceases to be able to operate efficiently.
Certain wage increases mean just transferring resources from the shareholder to the workers, but there is a point which, if you transfer any more, the company goes broke ...
I do not know whether the Prime Minister was thinking about General Motors, Chrysler or Ford, but there is not much chance they will go broke; there is perhaps more chance that the government of Canada will go broke than that the same would happen to General Motors.
Mr. Bain had some very interesting observations to make about the Prime Minister's speech. It is reputed that the Prime Minister does not read the newspapers, and I am sure he does not read Hansard, so he may not read what I say any more than what Mr. Bain writes, but I find it interesting because during the campaign Mr. Bain was full of admiration for the Prime Minister, as were most newspapermen. This is what Mr. Bain wrote:
Reactionary may not be the word. But the total effect of those words, to my mind, is to foster public prejudice against all wage demands in the public sector, without regard to whether a particular wage demand may be eminently justified to correct a gross inequity.
In other words, what Mr. Bain is saying is that if the Prime Minister thinks that the wage demands of the postal workers or of any other group of workers are exorbitant, he should say so and not blame all workers, as he did in this press interview, for being guilty of demanding exorbitant wage increases. I say the Prime Minister should adopt the same principle in both cases, that of the strikes and that of the price increases of the automobile manufacturers. He should give the people of Canada a lead. He should do as President Johnson has done and as President Kennedy did before him. He should say to the automobile companies of this country that they are big and efficient enough and that their profits are large enough so that they do not need the

September 19, 1968
Division
price increases which they have announced for the coming year.
When we talk about automobiles, we no longer refer to a luxury. Automobiles are a necessity in this day and age. In most cities of Canada workers often drive 10, 15 or 20 miles or more in each direction to go to work. Farmers need cars, and nearly every citizen of Canada feels he needs a car and buys one. It seems to me that if the Prime Minister and his government really believe in a just society, about which they talk so frequently and so eloquently, they should apply the principles, which one would expect in a just society, to the kind of case which I have tried to document today, namely the unnecessary and exorbitant increases which are being proposed in the prices of the 1969 automobiles by Chrysler and other corporations of Canada.
